units.title: Hell and Purgatory
intro: Auden’s list begins with Dante’s *Divine Comedy*, and he kept it in front of the class all term. When they came to Kafka, three months later, he told them to keep Dante in mind as they read.
This week is Hell and the mountain of Purgatory: sixty-seven cantos, in the prose translation he assigned or in Longfellow’s verse.

paras: This is the first of the nine operas on the list. Orpheus goes down among the dead while he is still alive, as Dante does, and he is allowed to bring one of them back on a condition. The libretto is thirteen pages and the opera lasts about an hour and a half. The record here is its best-known aria.

Gluck made two versions, the Italian (*Orfeo ed Euridice*, Vienna, 1762) and a longer French one (*Orphée et Eurydice*, Paris, 1774). Recordings of both are in three acts. The libretto printed here is in four, and its second and third acts make up the second act of a recording.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about opera
paras: Auden names Gluck’s *Orpheus* in two pieces of 1948, an article for *Vogue* and the introduction to a book of Greek writers, both times as the point where a period starts. Nothing more by him about the opera has been found. The introduction, “The Greeks and Us,” says that Athenian drama, in its seventy-five or so years, is outdone by “the golden age of European opera” as a period of continuous work in a single art. It counts that age as the hundred and twenty-five years from Gluck’s *Orpheus* to Verdi’s *Otello*, and the *Vogue* article gives the years, 1762 and 1887. All nine operas on the list were first performed within those years.

“Notes on Music and Opera” is an essay in Auden’s book *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). It dates opera’s great years from Mozart to Verdi (the introduction of 1948 began them with Gluck) and says that liberal humanism was at its height in the same years, when people believed without question in freedom and progress. Auden suggests that if good operas are rarer in his own time, the cause may be that people have learned they are not as free as the humanists supposed and have come to doubt whether being free makes people good. But opera would become impossible only if people stopped believing in free will and personality altogether. “Every high C accurately struck demolishes the theory that we are the irresponsible puppets of fate or chance.”
sources: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 8.
“Opera Addict,” written for *Vogue* in 1948, in *Prose, Volume II*, pp. 400–402.

questions.text: No one in Dante’s Hell asks to be let out. Why not?
gloss: Begin with the crowd on the bank of Acheron at the end of Canto III, and with what Virgil says of them.

paras: No essay by Auden on the *Comedy* itself has been found, but he touches on this question in his introduction to a selection from Søren Kierkegaard that was published in 1952. Kierkegaard is the Danish religious writer whose *Fear and Trembling* is assigned in week 6.

According to the Kierkegaard introduction, the relation of each creature to the God of the Bible cannot be broken. Auden says that people may try to put the relation out of their minds but do not get rid of it by doing so; they still feel it, as guilt and despair. On this view the wrath of God does not describe a feeling in God but the way God appears to anyone who distorts or denies that relation.

Auden says that this is why Dante could write over the gate that Hell was made by Power, Wisdom and Love. He adds that the English writer Walter Savage Landor was right to remark that the people in the *Inferno* do not want to get out. Auden does not say how the remark follows from the rest. As this site reads the passage, the damned would have to stop denying their relation to God before they could ask to be let out.
sources: “Søren Kierkegaard,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 176.

questions.text: How can people be blamed for what they love?
gloss: Dante asks this himself in *Purgatorio* XVIII. Virgil has just told him, in XVII, that love is the seed in us of every virtue and of every act that deserves punishment.

paras: “Balaam and His Ass,” an essay in Auden’s book *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), is about masters and servants in literature. In the essay Caliban, the wild islander enslaved by the magician Prospero in Shakespeare’s *The Tempest*, represents nature. Auden says that the play, which you will read in week 5, treats nature as the guilty party in the quarrel between nature and spirit, and spirit as blameless. Dante’s view is “the exact opposite.” For that view Auden quotes three lines from Virgil’s speech in *Purgatorio* XVII. The lines say that natural love cannot go wrong, but that the other love, the love a mind chooses, can go wrong in three ways: it takes a bad object, or it has too much force, or too little.

Auden comments that a merely natural creature cannot want more or less than is good for it, since excess and shortage are equally painful to it. Animals cannot fall, because the tempter’s promise, “Ye shall be as gods,” is in the future tense, which animals do not have.
Auden does not himself apply the lines to the question. This site does, and takes them to mean that people can be blamed for a love they have chosen.
sources: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 130–132.

making.title: A chart of Hell
making.short: Ten places: who is there, and what is done to them
brief: Fill in this chart from the poem alone, without looking at notes or a commentary. If you lose your way, read Canto XI, where Virgil stops and explains the plan. He counts only the three circles below him, so his first and second circles are the seventh and eighth of this chart and his smallest circle is the ninth.

The chart of Hell is the site’s. The chart Auden made for his students was of the themes of the course. Donald Pearce, a student in the class who wrote down after lectures what he could remember, describes Auden copying it out across the whole blackboard. You will fill in that chart in week 15.
rules: For each place, say who is punished there and what the punishment is.
Keep each entry to a line or two.

The seventh circle has three rings and the eighth has ten ditches. Fill in those two rows ring by ring and ditch by ditch, for as many as you can. The entries in those rows may run longer than two lines.
Fill at least sixteen of the twenty boxes. You can then finish, and the site shows the chart as the poem has it.

key.title: The chart, from the poem

rows.who: Those who lived without blame and without praise, and the angels who took neither side.
rows.what: They run after a banner that never stops, stung by flies and wasps.

rows.who: The unbaptized, and the great of the ancient world.
rows.what: No torment. They live in desire without hope.

rows.who: The lustful.
rows.what: A storm drives them through the dark and never rests.

rows.who: The gluttons.
rows.what: They lie in mud under rain, hail and snow. Cerberus tears them.

rows.who: The hoarders and the spendthrifts.
rows.what: They roll great weights against each other, and each side shouts at the other.

rows.who: The angry and the sullen.
rows.what: The angry tear at each other in the marsh of Styx. The sullen lie under its mud.

rows.who: The heretics.
The violent, in three rings: against their neighbors; against themselves; against God, nature and art.
rows.what: In the same order: sunk in a river of boiling blood; turned into trees in a wood, where those who destroyed their own goods are hunted by dogs; kept on burning sand under a rain of fire.

rows.who: The fraudulent, in ten ditches: panders and seducers; flatterers; sellers of church offices; soothsayers; sellers of public offices; hypocrites; thieves; false counselors; sowers of discord; falsifiers.
rows.what: In the same order: whipped by demons; sunk in filth; set head down in holes with their soles on fire; their heads twisted backward; boiled in pitch; cloaked in gilded lead; bitten by serpents and changed into them; wrapped in flame; cut open with a sword; wasted by disease.

rows.who: The traitors: to kin, to country, to guests, to lords and benefactors.
rows.what: They are fixed in the ice of Cocytus. At the center Satan chews Judas, Brutus and Cassius.

after: Virgil gives the plan in Canto XI. The second, third, fourth and fifth circles lie outside the city of Dis and punish incontinence, that is, lack of self-control. The seventh circle punishes violence, and the eighth and ninth punish fraud. Virgil’s plan does not place the first circle or the sixth.

making.reflect: Choose one circle. What does the punishment have to do with the sin?

meetings.title: A speech in Hell
meetings.blurb: A man in Hell tells how he talked his crew into one more voyage. Nine words are missing from what he says.

lead: Nine words have been taken out. Write in each gap the word you think Longfellow used. Do it before you open the book. Nothing depends on being right.

notes.0: The first thing he tells us is their age. What he asks next, he asks of men with little left to lose.
notes.1: A world with nobody in it. There is no one out there to rob, rule or trade with. The only thing the voyage offers is the knowing.
notes.2: He appeals to their breeding: remember the stock you come from. You will meet the word again on the mountain, where Virgil calls love the seed of every virtue and of every act that deserves punishment (*Purgatorio* XVII).
notes.3: Men on one side, beasts on the other, and nothing between. It flatters them. It also leaves out everyone who stays at home and is not a beast.
notes.4: He is reporting his own success. Fifteen lines earlier these men were *old and slow*. One short speech, and they cannot be held back.
notes.5: The oars become wings: the ship is trying to fly. His verdict on the flying comes in the same line.
notes.6: This is his own word for the voyage, said in Hell with the voyage long over. The Italian is *folle*. Dante uses the same word of his own journey, at the start of the poem, when he is afraid to begin it (*Inferno* II).
notes.7: The line turns over in the middle. They have seen land for the first time in five months, and the land kills them.
notes.8: He does not say who. Ulysses is a pagan, dead a thousand years before Christ, and has no name for the one who sank him. Keep the phrase in mind for the first canto of the *Purgatorio*.

after: Ulysses is Homer’s Odysseus. In Homer he gets home. This last voyage is found in no earlier poet and seems to be Dante’s own invention.

Auden grants the likeness. But look at where Dante has put the man who says it.

reply: That is the charge against him. He is in the eighth circle, with those who used the gift of speech to deceive, and this speech is the gift at work: men who had come through *a hundred thousand perils* are dead within the page.
But Dante gives him the best lines in the canto, and when he stops speaking neither Dante nor Virgil says a word against him.

Ulysses tells his crew what they were made for, and it is the same offer: knowledge, and a higher rank in creation than the one they have.

steps.title: What Auden made of Ulysses
paras: Auden wrote about this passage in *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950), three lectures on the sea in the writing of the Romantics. Dante’s Ulysses, he says, behaves as the sea-going hero of the Romantic writers does, and Tennyson made him one.
But to Dante, Auden adds, the voyage was the sin of Adam, and the speech to the crew echoes what the Serpent said to Eve.

The poem keeps both readings open. Dante uses Ulysses’ word for the voyage, *folle*, of his own journey. The mountain that Ulysses drowned in sight of is taken by nearly every commentator to be the one Dante climbs in the *Purgatorio*. And from high in Paradise Dante looks down at the strait once more and sees “the mad track of Ulysses” (*Paradiso* XXVII). Ulysses went where Dante goes, and went without being sent.
sources: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 10. The third paragraph is this site’s, from the places in the poem that it names.

Natural or spiritual; and thou knowest it.

steps.title: The other descent: Gluck’s *Orpheus*
paras: Auden put nine operas on the reading list of a course in literature, and he brought a portable phonograph to class and played records to make his points.

Orpheus is let into the underworld alive because of his singing. He may lead Eurydice out on one condition, that he does not look at her on the way. Dante is led down by Virgil and may look at everything.
This record is the aria Orpheus sings when he has looked, and she has died a second time. Its first words mean *What shall I do without Eurydice?* Play it before you go on.

options.label: Grief.
reply: Most listeners since 1762 have heard it so, and it is the best-known thing Gluck wrote. Now try to say what in the sound is sad. The key is major, and nothing in the tune breaks or cries out.

options.label: Something too calm for what has just happened.
reply: Listeners in Gluck’s own day said the same.

options.label: I could not tell from the tune. The words would have to say.
reply: That is the oldest complaint made against this aria.

after: In 1854 the critic Eduard Hanslick repeated a remark made by a contemporary of Gluck’s: the tune would go as well, or better, with the opposite words, *I have found my Eurydice*.

steps.title: What Auden said about suffering in opera
paras: In “Notes on Music and Opera” Auden says that in a sense there can be no tragic opera. Whatever the characters suffer and whatever mistakes they make, “they are doing exactly what they wish.”
Opera, he says in the same essay, imitates human willfulness. We have feelings, and we insist on having them whatever they cost us.
Orpheus was told not to look, and he looked. Paolo and Francesca, in the second circle of Hell, are still together.

questions.text: The hero of the play you read had to choose between two courses. Was either of them right? Is the hero guilty, and of what?

paras: Auden wrote about the Greek tragic hero in 1948, in the introduction to a collection of Greek writers in translation.

In that introduction he says that the hero of Homer is a model for a ruling class to copy, but that the hero of tragedy is a warning to the ordinary citizens of the chorus. The tragic hero, he writes, begins in glory and ends by suffering more than those citizens do. As a rule, the wrong the hero does is one that could not have been avoided: Agamemnon must kill his daughter or fail his army, and Antigone must fail her dead brother or her city.

According to Auden, the Greeks concluded that anyone caught in such a position was already guilty of a further fault, hubris, which is the confidence of the fortunate that they are like gods and cannot be made to suffer. Sometimes, Auden says, the hero shows it in an act, as Agamemnon does when he walks on the purple cloth. Where no act shows it, the hubris is assumed, since otherwise the gods would not be punishing the hero.

Auden calls the world of Greek tragedy foreign to modern readers. They take what a person does to be partly that person’s own choice and partly circumstances, and they cannot make sense of a situation that by itself makes a person guilty. He gives the example of Oedipus, who killed his father and married his mother without knowing who they were. Sophocles tells the story in *Oedipus the King*, a play that is not on the list. A modern playwright, Auden says, would show Oedipus tempted and deceiving himself, and so answerable for what follows. Of the Oedipus that Sophocles wrote, nobody can say, “That was where he made his fatal mistake.”
sources: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 18–21.

questions.text: In *Odes* I.3 Horace prays for the ship in which his friend Virgil, the poet who guides Dante, is sailing to Greece. Then Horace says that whoever first went to sea broke a law of the gods. What, for Horace, is wrong with going to sea?
gloss: Read I.3 and I.14 together.

paras: In 1949 Auden lectured at the University of Virginia on the sea in Romantic literature. The lectures were published as *The Enchafèd Flood*. The first of them sets out what the sea meant to writers before the Romantics, whom he dates from the late eighteenth century.

In Genesis and in one Greek story of how the world began, he says, the sea is what was there before anything had a form. It is the disorder that civilization emerged from and can fall back into. For that reason, he says, writers made a ship stand for the state only when the state was in danger, since a ship ought to be in harbor. In ordinary times society is pictured as a city or a garden, the places where people belong. As an example of the ship in danger Auden quotes *Odes* I.14, where Horace calls to a ship that the waves are carrying out again and tells it to make for port.

A voyage is therefore a necessary evil, Auden says: Homer’s Odysseus is only trying to get home, and Jason, the Greek hero sent to bring back the Golden Fleece, would be glad if it were nearer. The lecture quotes *Odes* I.3 to show that for a classical writer nobody goes to sea who can stay ashore, and that the attempt to cross the sea “betrays a rashness bordering on hubris.” Hubris is the Greek word for the pride of people who believe they are like gods.

After Horace, Auden writes about Dante’s Ulysses (Odysseus under his Latin name), whom you met in week 1, then about Shakespeare, and then about the Romantics, for whom every person of feeling and honor longs to get away from land and city. Keep Horace’s view in mind until you reach *Moby-Dick*, Herman Melville’s novel of a whaling voyage, in weeks 11 to 13.
sources: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 6–12.

making.title: A poem from the Latin
making.short: Eight lines of Horace and a word list
brief: At Michigan Auden had each student translate a poem from German, French or Latin. Students picked a language they had not studied and were allowed no help but a dictionary.
The poem printed below is *Odes* I.11, in which Horace addresses a woman who has been consulting astrologers. The word list takes the place of the dictionary.
rules: Make an English poem of the ode. The Latin has eight long lines, and your version may have more than eight but not fewer.

Work from the word list alone, with no dictionary. You may use English words that are not in the list. Latin puts words in an order English cannot keep, so the notes in the word list say which words belong together, and the sense must tell you the rest.

Until you have finished, do not look at any translation and do not open Book I of the *Odes* in this week’s reading, where this ode is printed in English. John Conington’s translation of 1863 is shown when you finish.
If you have studied Latin, do this exercise anyway, and spend more time on the translation from French in week 10 or from German in week 14.

making.title: Thirteen lines of terza rima
brief: Dante wrote the *Comedy* in terza rima, in which the lines are grouped in threes, called tercets. The middle line of each tercet gives the rhyme for the first and third lines of the next, so that each tercet is locked to the one after it. Each canto ends on a single line that closes the last rhyme. The first nine lines of the poem are printed below in Italian. You do not need Italian to see the pattern: look at the last word of each line.
Longfellow’s translation kept the tercets and gave up the rhyme, and the prose translation Auden assigned gave up the lines as well. Write thirteen lines of terza rima in English.
rules: Thirteen lines: four tercets and a closing line, rhymed aba bcb cdc ded e.
Any subject. Ten syllables to a line is usual in English.
Do not end a sentence at the end of every tercet. Let at least one sentence run on from one tercet into the next.

auden.title: What Auden wrote, and said in class
paras: In 1944 Auden reviewed a book from the list of recommended reading, C. N. Cochrane’s *Christianity and Classical Culture*. Much of the review is about Augustine.

Auden says in the review that the classical philosophers thought of a person as divine reason shut up in a body. They put evil in the body, and held that to know the truth was to be free of evil. Augustine, he says, replaced this picture with another, in which people are made in the image of God and are fallen. A person is still divided in Augustine’s picture, but not into mind and body. The division now falls between the flesh, by which Auden means mind and body together in their self-loving state, and the spirit, which bears witness to what a person is still meant to be.

From this division Auden concludes that a Christian such as Augustine, writing on ethics, begins with neither a reasonable act nor a pleasant one but with the gratuitous act. Such an act is done only to show that the people who do it are their own masters. He quotes Dostoevsky, the novelist you will read in weeks 7 to 10, whose hero in *Notes from Underground* protests that there is no free will left for a person whose wishes can be worked out by arithmetic. People act, Auden says, either out of love of self, “just for the hell of it,” or out of love of God, “just for the heaven of it,” and their reasons and appetites come second.

One of the answers Augustine gives in Book II is that he wanted the theft itself and not the fruit. The review does not mention the pears. Auden spoke of them three years later, in a lecture on *Othello* given in New York in 1947. In the students’ notes from which that lecture has been reconstructed, he says that the idea of the gratuitous act first appears in the *Confessions*, where Augustine tells of robbing the pear tree.

Donald Pearce, a student in Auden’s class at Michigan in 1941, wrote down after lectures what he could remember. His notes preserve part of a lecture on the ego in Augustine and in Franz Kafka, whose novel *The Castle* is assigned in weeks 14 and 15. Auden called Augustine the subtlest observer of his own mind between Aristotle and Freud. Augustine’s account of the conflict between self and ego, he said, matters less now as psychology than as ethics, where it must always be “an archetypal text.”
sources: “Augustus to Augustine,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 34 and 36–37.
W. H. Auden, *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (Princeton University Press, 2000), the lecture on *Othello*.
Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” p. 134.

paras: Auden writes about Augustine and time in “Balaam and His Ass,” an essay on masters and servants collected in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). The passage comes in his account of Phileas Fogg, the hero of Jules Verne’s novel *Around the World in Eighty Days*, whom Auden describes as a worshipper of the clock.

According to the essay, the ancients for the most part thought of time as a pendulum or a wheel, so that sooner or later everything recurs and nothing can happen once and for all. The idea of a single event at a single moment cannot be drawn from the outside world, where every movement swings or circles, but only from the inner experience of remembering and looking forward. The essay credits Augustine with the first serious study of that experience.

Auden then says that time seen from outside is Fate or Chance, the part of people’s lives that they are not answerable for and can do nothing about. Seen from inside, their time is their own, and they feel answerable for it. He adds that the Stoics of the ancient world trained themselves to master their passions but did not think of mastering their time, because they did not know that it was theirs. Auden calls Fogg a modern Stoic, who masters his passions by mastering his time.

This site wrote the question so that you would have to choose between the two views of time in Auden’s essay. A past that happened to you is time seen from outside, and a past that you are doing now is time seen from inside.
sources: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 140–141.

auden.title: What Auden said in class, and wrote later
paras: Auden told the class to take no notes, so Donald Pearce, one of the students, wrote down after lectures what he could remember. The next two paragraphs are from his notes.

Iago, Auden said, is cold and cannot love other people, and has learned to make a strength of this lack. He is the only brilliant person in *Othello*, with what the French writer Pascal calls the geometrical mind (the mathematical mind, in the translation assigned in week 5), and he settles every question by reasoning alone. Auden thought it significant that Iago alone in the play shows any knowledge of the Bible, and went on to call him “the villain as inverted saint,” a man who at bottom wanted to be a saint. In the saint and in the villain “Ethics and Esthetics have become almost the same thing,” and both are free of the scruples that govern most people’s dealings with others.

The next lecture began: “Falstaff is a comic edition of Iago.” The two are alike, Auden said, in leaving right and wrong out of their dealings with people. Each keeps life at arm’s length without seeming to, Iago in the manner of a scientist and Falstaff in the manner of a playwright. In these lectures Falstaff is an opportunist without a conscience and a disappointed man, who drinks to swallow his disappointments and plays the child so as not to be hurt. Auden called Prince Hal an unfeeling Machiavel, or schemer, who like Iago is thought honest and sociable and like Iago is expert at deceiving. Hal has no personal ties and Falstaff has no other kind, and so the break between them could not be avoided.

Auden did not keep this view of Falstaff. In “The Prince’s Dog,” an essay he collected in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), he asks why, whenever Falstaff is on the stage, nobody looks at Hal. He answers that *Henry IV* is also a parable. On the surface, he says, Falstaff is a Lord of Misrule, the mock ruler who presides over holiday revels. In the parable he is a comic symbol of charity in its older sense of love, and Prince Hal stands for worldly justice. In “The Joker in the Pack,” an essay on *Othello* in the same book, Auden describes Iago as a practical joker. Every deed in the play, he says, is Iago’s, and the other characters perform no actions of their own but only behave.
sources: Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” pp. 134 and 142–148.
“The Prince’s Dog” and “The Joker in the Pack,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 198, 246 and 253.

paras: Auden wrote a short note on Hamlet and Don Quixote, the hero of Cervantes’s novel. It is one of several notes on Don Quixote in “Genius & Apostle,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962).

Hamlet, the note says, has no faith in God and none in himself, and so he can say who he is only by what other people have done: he is the man whose uncle murdered his father and then married his mother. He envies the heroes of Greek tragedy, who are made what they are by their situation. That envy, the note says, is why Hamlet cannot act. He can only “act” in the player’s sense, and try one possibility after another. Auden had written in 1948, in “The Greeks and Us,” his introduction to a book of Greek writers, that in a Greek tragedy the situation by itself can make a hero guilty.
The note contrasts Hamlet with Don Quixote, who believes he is a knight and cannot see himself as playing a part at all, and is therefore the opposite of an actor.

paras: “The Globe,” an essay in Auden’s book *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), is about the Elizabethan stage, and in it he writes: “In a Greek tragedy everything that could have been otherwise has already happened before the play begins.” In an Elizabethan tragedy, the essay goes on, the hero can still turn back. Othello, for example, could at any point before the murder have governed his jealousy, learned the truth and given the play a happy ending.

Auden’s essay on *Othello*, in the same book, says that Othello is brought down by another man and originates nothing himself, so that an audience pities him without respecting him and saves what Auden calls its aesthetic respect for Iago.

Auden had taken a different view in 1948, in “The Greeks and Us,” his introduction to a book of Greek writers, where he called Othello a tragic hero in the modern sense. In Greek tragedy, he wrote, heroes suffer a punishment sent from outside, and by bearing it they are reconciled to the law in the end. The suffering that a modern audience finds tragic is suffering that heroes make for themselves and insist on, and so they die defiant and unreconciled.
sources: “The Globe” and “The Joker in the Pack,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 174–175 and 246–247.

In that version the spoken scenes are shortened and sung, and the English shortens them in the same way, so a recording in German has more speech in it than you will find on the page. The English of most of the arias follows the German words.

While you listen, compare Tamino, a prince, with Papageno, the bird-catcher who is sent along with him. Tamino goes through the trials of the temple. In a spoken scene that the page leaves out, Papageno says that he wants no wisdom and is then talked into the first trial. He fails it, and in Act 2, Scene 8 he is content to go no further. Notice what each is given at the end.
The words are by Emanuel Schikaneder, who also sang Papageno at the first performance, in Vienna in 1791.

Auden compares this opera with *The Tempest* in “Balaam and His Ass,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). According to the essay, each work has a pair, one who stands for spirit and one who stands for nature: Prospero and Caliban, Tamino and Papageno. In the play the two are at war and the blame is put on nature, and Auden calls that too gloomy.

The opera he calls too hopeful. In it the two live side by side without a quarrel. Tamino earns his reward by daring the trials at the risk of his life, and Papageno earns his by being humble enough to refuse them. That refusal, Auden says, is as if Caliban had thanked Prospero for the offer of an education and declined it, preferring to stay in the jungle without clothes or speech.
Auden made an English version of *The Magic Flute* with Chester Kallman, the American poet who was his partner in writing opera libretti. It was broadcast on American television in January 1956.
sources: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 130 and 134–135.

questions.text: How has Prospero erred?
gloss: Auden asked this question in his lecture on the play in December 1941, near the end of the term. Look at the whole play: how Prospero lost Milan (he tells it in Act 1, Scene 2), how he rules the island, and what he gives up at the end.

auden.title: What Auden said in class, and wrote later
paras: Auden answered the question himself. Donald Pearce, a student in the class, wrote down after lectures what he could remember, and his account gives the answer. Prospero, Auden said, erred by neglecting the daily work of governing Milan. He wanted to perfect himself in secret studies, which he found more exciting than public duty. Auden thought it quite proper that Prospero’s brother turned him out. On the island, Auden said, Prospero learns magic, but he also learns what matters more, that the art of life is to meet the ordinary claims of living. So he gives up his magic and goes home. Auden compared this with the end of Goethe’s *Faust* (in the second part, which is not on the list), where Faust gives up knowledge and power to help build dikes.

In the same lecture Auden took the play as Shakespeare’s testament, a summing-up of what he had come to think. Miranda and Ferdinand, he said, are Shakespeare’s last word on love, and love here is a plain thing that leads to marriage and children. Gonzalo is another Polonius, the old counselor in *Hamlet*, but one whom Shakespeare now respects, while the clever villains of the earlier plays have shrunk to Antonio and his hangers-on. Pearce gives Auden’s conclusion as “For the purposes of normal human life, the gentle, honest soul is best.”

Three years after the course Auden published a long poem, *The Sea and the Mirror*, in which the people of the play speak after it is over. His judgment of the play in prose is in “Balaam and His Ass,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), which calls *The Tempest* “a disquieting work.” According to that essay, only Alonso seems truly sorry. The others repent as people do who have been punished and frightened, and Prospero pardons them with contempt, knowing that he has them in his power. Auden says that a reader must admire Prospero but cannot like him. Prospero is cold, and the thought that he might himself have done wrong and need pardon never crosses his mind.

The essay gives Caliban the better of the argument. Before Prospero came, Auden writes, the island was Caliban’s alone, and he lived there in the innocence of a savage. Prospero tried to educate him, gave it up when Caliban tried to rape Miranda, and then, instead of letting him go back to the forest, kept him as a slave and ruled him by fear. Prospero gets his fire made and his wood fetched, and Auden cannot see what Caliban gets in return.
sources: Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” pp. 148–152.

questions.text: At the end of *Volpone* the guilty are punished and nobody is forgiven. Is the play a comedy?
gloss: The court sentences Volpone, Mosca and the others in the last scene. Jonson expected readers to object that so harsh an ending does not suit a comedy, and he answers them in the Epistle printed before the play.

paras: “The Globe,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), is an essay about the Elizabethan stage. Auden says in it that Jonson owes less to Latin comedy than to the morality play of the Middle Ages. (In a morality play, vices and virtues fight over one figure who stands for all mankind. In the best-known example the figure is called Everyman.) The pattern of a comedy by Jonson, he writes, is the morality with one of the seven deadly sins put where Everyman stood, and the other six making what they can out of him.

Later in the essay he divides comedy into two kinds. Classical comedy sorts mankind into those who have excellence and those who have none, and only the second sort, the fools and rascals and slaves, can be laughed at. Its rascals get the beating they deserve, and at the end, Auden says, the audience laughs while the people on the stage weep.

According to the essay, Christian comedy holds that everyone is a sinner, so nobody is too good to be shown up. It also holds that all are forbidden to judge one another and commanded to forgive. Its people are exposed and then pardoned, and at the curtain they are laughing with the audience.

Jonson’s comedies, he says, are classical, but Shakespeare’s are Christian. In your reply, compare the last scene of *Volpone* with the last scene of *The Tempest* and say whether the difference holds.
sources: “The Globe,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 173 and 177.

questions.text: Pascal says that you must bet on whether God exists, and that reason cannot settle the bet for you. Can a person come to believe a thing by deciding that it pays to believe it?
gloss: The wager is no. 233, in Section III. Read to the end of it, where Pascal answers people who say they are so made that they cannot believe.

paras: In 1952 Auden introduced a selection from Søren Kierkegaard, the Danish religious writer whom you read next week. In that introduction he says that no argument can make a person believe, and that nobody can make the choice for another. He finds that neither Pascal’s “wager” nor Kierkegaard’s “leap” (his word for the step into faith) quite describes that choice, because the first sounds like prudent calculation and the second like willfulness. The wager, he grants, does remind people that in every other part of life they act on faith all the time, and willingly, so that they cannot expect religion to be different. The leap reminds them that everybody lives by faith in something, and that people whose faith gives way must jump, even if they cannot see where they will land.

In *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962) he writes that accounts of choice like the wager and the leap “are interesting as dramatic literature, but are they true?” Of the few choices that decided his own life, he finds that at the time he did not know how serious they were. What had seemed a brook turned out to have been a Rubicon. He is thankful for that ignorance, because if he had known the risk he would never have dared.
sources: “Søren Kierkegaard,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 178–179.
“Hic et Ille,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 103.

making.short: Give each part a voice, and say why
brief: In New York in 1946 and 1947 Auden gave a course on Shakespeare at the New School. He offered different projects to students who acted, designed for the stage or wrote. Those who wrote poems or plays were to make an opera libretto out of a comedy or a tragedy. One of the problems this raises, he noted, is the distribution of voices.
Do that part of the work for *The Tempest*: decide what kind of voice is to sing each part. A part given to a bass is a different part from the same words given to a tenor.
There is no one right casting of the play.
rules: Give each part a voice: soprano, mezzo-soprano, contralto, tenor, baritone or bass. The first three are women’s voices and the last three are men’s, each listed from high to low. A part may also be spoken, or danced, or cut.
Say why in a line. Go by what the character is in the play, and not by any singer you have heard.
Prospero, Ariel and Caliban must have three different voices.

Each part has two boxes, one for a voice and one for a reason, twenty-two in all. Try to fill every one. If you cut a part, write that in its voice box and give the reason. The site lets you finish once sixteen boxes are filled, and then shows how Mozart cast *The Magic Flute*.

paras: *Don Giovanni* takes close to three hours. It is sung in Italian. In the English printed here the hero is called Don Juan, and the text stops where he is dragged down to hell, after the statue of the Commandant, whom he killed in the first scene, has come to supper. On the stage a short last scene follows, in which the others come back and are told what has happened.
While you listen, follow Leporello, Don Giovanni’s servant, and decide which of the two men is the master.
The words are by Lorenzo Da Ponte, and the opera was first performed in Prague in 1787.

In “Balaam and His Ass,” an essay on masters and servants printed in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden denies that desire is what sends Don Giovanni after women. A sensual man, he says, goes after the women who are his type and turns his eyes from one who is plain and elderly, whereas Leporello says of his master that rich or poor, ugly or beautiful, any woman will do so long as she wears a skirt. Auden calls the Don’s pleasure “arithmetical,” because what satisfies him is one more name for his list. He therefore wants the Don to look as unremarkable on the stage as possible, so that the audience understands that stamps would have served him as well as women.

Auden adds that a merely sensual man has no need of a servant, and that the Don can be understood only together with his servant. Leporello keeps the list, and only Leporello is ever seen to take pleasure in it. By the end of the opera, Auden says, a listener begins to suspect that Leporello was the master all along. He wonders whether the statue ought to have dragged Leporello down to hell and left the Don to die in peace.
sources: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 119–120.

auden.title: What Auden said in class, and wrote later
paras: Donald Pearce, a student in the class, opens his account of the course on a Thursday afternoon late in October 1941, with Auden lecturing on Kierkegaard. Auden set out three ways of judging an act. Kierkegaard, he told the class, treats the first two at length. The aesthetic asks how interesting the act is. A theft of a million dollars by a millionaire is of no interest, Auden said, but a theft of eleven cents by a millionaire is interesting. The ethical cares only for what all thefts have in common, and has no place for the exception. The third way is the religious, and in it, Auden said, the other two meet. Like the aesthetic it has to do with the particular case, here and now, and like the ethical it keeps the larger whole in view. His example was a man who would like to kiss a woman married to someone else. The aesthetic lets him if his passion is real and he can make it interesting, the ethical forbids him and tells him to take a sedative, and the religious forbids him the kiss and the sedative too. Pearce’s account does not mention Abraham, whose case in *Fear and Trembling* is of the third kind.

Auden wrote out the same three ways in 1952, in his introduction to a selection from Kierkegaard, where he applies them to religion. He takes the Greek gods as his example of an aesthetic religion and the God of the Greek philosophers as his example of an ethical one. In the first the gods give orders as they please and no two orders are alike, so the orders can never be made into a code. The second expects its commands to form a complete code of laws that hold for everyone. The command of the God of the Bible, he says, is of neither kind. It is the call of duty, “Choose to do what at this moment in this context I am telling you to do.”

Auden writes of such a call again in “Genius & Apostle,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). People of genius, he says, are called by a gift they were born with, and so what they must do and what they want to do are the same. An apostle’s call comes straight from God. One of Auden’s two examples is God’s command to Abraham to leave his own country, which comes earlier in Genesis than the command to sacrifice Isaac. Nobody can explain why the call came to Abraham and not to someone else, the essay says, and no natural desire of Abraham’s can have answered to it. An apostle, in Auden’s words, has to say, “I would not but, alas, I must.”
sources: Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” pp. 129–131.
“Søren Kierkegaard,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 172–177.

questions.text: Kierkegaard’s knight of faith looks like a shopkeeper out for a walk. Nothing in his looks gives his faith away. How then does he differ from the shopkeeper?
gloss: The portrait is in the last of the four parts printed here. Kierkegaard compares the knight of faith with another knight, the knight of infinite resignation.

paras: Reviewing the first volume of Kierkegaard’s *Journals and Papers* in 1968, Auden says that Kierkegaard was a Manichee in his feelings, though never in his doctrine. (The Manichees held that the material world was made by an evil spirit.) Kierkegaard would not have denied that God made the world, Auden says, yet his writings never give the feeling that to be alive, whatever a person suffers, is a blessing. Kierkegaard heard one theme of the New Testament, suffering and self-sacrifice, with unusual sharpness and was deaf to the rest. Against him Auden quotes Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the German pastor whom the Nazis hanged in 1945. If God grants people some great earthly happiness, Bonhoeffer wrote, “we ought not to try and be more religious than God Himself.”

Auden grants that Kierkegaard could not truthfully have said those words of himself. What amazes Auden in the portrait of the knight of faith is the evidence that Kierkegaard knew he could not, and counted that a fault rather than a virtue. As Auden describes him, the knight has a happy marriage, the look of a cheerful grocer and the respect of his neighbors. Kierkegaard, he points out, calls this what a person ought to be, and admits that he cannot understand such a man.

Auden makes a passing remark about the knight in an essay on Sydney Smith, an English clergyman and wit of the early nineteenth century. What Kierkegaard chiefly held against the respectable middle class, he says, was that it parodied the knight of faith. The remark does not say what the knight has that a parody of him lacks. For that, go back to the portrait and find what Kierkegaard says the knight is doing at every moment, though nothing of it shows.
sources: “A Knight of Doleful Countenance,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 191–192.
“Portrait of a Whig,” in the same book, p. 167.

questions.text: Phaedra says that her love for her stepson is the work of Venus. Suppose there is no Venus. What has happened to her, and who is to blame?
gloss: She says so in her first scene, in Act 1. Her last speech is in Act 5.

paras: In “Writing,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden confesses that French classical tragedy strikes him as “opera for the unmusical.” Shakespeare, he says, can move readers who do not even hear the lines in their heads. He compares reading Racine silently to going through an opera score with too little skill to play or sing it, and holds that nobody who has not heard a great performance of *Phèdre* can form a fair idea of the play.

In the *Hippolytus* of Euripides, the Greek play on the same story, Auden recognizes a world akin to Shakespeare’s, where Aphrodite (the Greek name of Venus) cares as much for fish and birds as for human beings. Racine’s Venus, he says, cares nothing for animals, or for the lower classes either. Racine’s world has no weather and no nature in it, and Auden cannot imagine anyone in it sneezing. He concludes that passions like theirs have no life off the stage, and that it takes the voices and gestures of great actors to give them one.

In “The Globe,” an essay about the Elizabethan stage in the same book, Auden doubts whether a Christian society, which does not hold that suffering must be a sign of guilt, can have a wholly satisfactory tragedy. A dramatist in such a society, he says, can make the character who suffers noble and innocent, and then the effect is pathos and not tragedy. Or the sinners can bring the suffering on themselves, and then they cannot be noble, since it is sinning that makes a person ignoble. Shakespeare and Racine both try to get around the difficulty by putting noble verse in the sinner’s mouth. Auden calls this “a conjuring trick” and thinks both poets knew it was one. He adds that the story of Sophocles’ Oedipus would still be tragic if a journalist told it, but that the story of Shakespeare’s Macbeth would then be “a police court case” and Phaedra’s “a pathological case.”
sources: “Writing” and “The Globe,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 25–26 and 176.

auden.title: What Auden wrote in 1939 and after
paras: In the summer of 1939 Auden worked on a prose book that he left unfinished and that was published only after his death. He took its title, *The Prolific and the Devourer*, from Blake’s *Marriage*, and told a friend that he was writing a new *Marriage of Heaven and Hell*. He studied Pascal that summer, and began to call the book his *pensées*.

In the book Auden says that Pascal is to him what Montaigne was to Pascal. (Montaigne is the French essayist of the sixteenth century. Nos. 62 to 65 of the *Pensées*, in Section II, show a Pascal who cannot stop reading him and cannot forgive him.) He calls Pascal “incomparably the noblest and most seductive” of the dualists. A dualist, as the book uses the word, holds that everything is divided into a good part and an evil part, as into God and Satan or soul and body. Pascal, he says, did what most people do and valued what he lacked, the heart, above what he had, the reason. He concludes, “By all appearances he should have been damned, but he was saved, and saved not as he thought by his heart but by his reason,” and the ground he gives is that Pascal learned from his reason how corrupt his heart was, and so learned that human love was not for him.

In 1940 Auden cited Blake against the dualists. A note to *New Year Letter*, the long poem he wrote that year, says that everything the Devil teaches begins by dividing a whole from its parts, or one part of it from the rest. Dualism, the note says, comes from thinking about the creation as if it were governed the way people govern one another, and Auden credits Blake with having seen this. (The Devil of the note is not the Devil of Blake’s book, who argues against dividing body from soul.)

Auden had not come to Pascal fresh in 1939. In 1955 he wrote an essay, which has no title, for *Modern Canterbury Pilgrims*, a book of essays by members of the Episcopal Church about how they came to it. He recalls there that in his school and university years Pascal was the one writer on theology he could read, and one who disturbed his complacency. Looking back, he finds in Pascal’s writings “a certain element of fake,” a romantic pleasure in being unhappy, which he thinks may well have been what drew him to them as a young man.
sources: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 31 and 47–48.
*New Year Letter* (Faber and Faber, 1941), note to line 560.

Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden* (Princeton University Press, 2017), pp. 390–392 and 398–399, for the letter and for the essay, which is in *Modern Canterbury Pilgrims*, edited by James A. Pike (1956).

questions.text: Baudelaire says that the dandy should live and sleep before a mirror. What does the dandy need the mirror for?
gloss: The dandy comes into *My Heart Laid Bare* several times. Collect what is said of him before you answer.

paras: The course list names the Random House edition of the journals, which is the translation by Christopher Isherwood, the English novelist and a friend of Auden’s. (The translation printed here is an earlier one, by Joseph Shipley.) When Isherwood revised his translation and it was published again in 1947, Auden wrote the introduction. He says in it that Baudelaire, faced with his own nature and with the society of his century, set up a pair of opposites for himself and held to them until shortly before he went mad. One of the pair is the dandy, who is the heroic individual. The other is the common mass, in which Baudelaire put Woman, the man of business and the Belgians.

The dandy, as Auden describes him, does not act and does not look for wisdom, and wants neither the admiration of other people nor the knowledge of God. All he wants is the consciousness of being himself and like nobody else. Auden calls him “the religious hero turned upside down,” and identifies him with Lucifer, the rebel who shows that he is free by disobeying every command, whether God’s, society’s or his own nature’s.

The act proper to the dandy, according to the introduction, is the gratuitous act, since only an act that nothing calls for can be wholly the doer’s own choice. In the review of 1944 reported in week 3, Auden says that a person who acts from self-love acts “just for the hell of it.” For another act of the kind, go back to that week and the pears that Augustine stole.

In 1944, in an essay on Tennyson, the English poet of Queen Victoria’s reign, Auden compares the two poets and calls Baudelaire the greater. He finds them alike underneath, since both were lonely men, anxious about their own existence. Baudelaire went further as a poet because he also had a first-rate critical intelligence, but the same intelligence misled him into making a religion of art, which Tennyson never did. Auden sets Baudelaire’s shocking pose beside the preaching and flag-waving in Tennyson, and judges that each was a way of managing without religious belief and that both end in disaster.
sources: Introduction to Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals*, translated by Christopher Isherwood (Marcel Rodd, 1947), pp. 18–20.
“Augustus to Augustine,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 37.

making.title: Ten proverbs of Hell
brief: In an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden describes the college he would found for poets. Its library would have no books of literary criticism in it, and the students would practice criticism in one way only, by writing parodies.
There are about seventy Proverbs of Hell in Blake’s book, most of them one sentence long. Many contradict a saying that everyone accepts. Find out how they are made, and then write ten more.
rules: Ten proverbs, each on a line of its own.
No proverb longer than fifteen words.
At least three must answer a saying you were brought up on. Say the opposite and make it sound true. You need not write the saying down.

Use things that can be seen, as Blake uses the plow, the cistern and the crow. The following words of his are barred, and their plurals with them: eternity, infinite, wisdom, energy, desire, heaven, hell.
making.reflect: Which of your ten do you believe?

paras: The opera runs close to four hours. It is in three acts, and you can hear one act at a sitting. The English printed here spells three of the names in its own way: Isolda, Brangaena and Kurvenal.

While you listen, notice what keeps the lovers apart in each act, and ask what they would do if nothing did. In the love duet of the second act, listen for how Wagner holds the lovers’ voices apart, phrase after phrase, and lets them sing in unison only when the duet ends. Auden pointed this out to the class and said that Wagner does it deliberately.

Auden lectured in the fall of 1941 on the psychology of romantic love. For his lectures on love that semester he assigned this libretto and the libretto of *Carmen* (the opera for week 8). He also assigned Shakespeare’s *Romeo and Juliet*, which the list does not include, and Denis de Rougemont’s *Love in the Western World*, then a new book, which the list only recommends. He ended the lecture on romantic love by playing the love duet on the small portable phonograph he often brought to class.

auden.title: What Auden said in class, and wrote later
paras: Donald Pearce, a student in the class who wrote down after lectures what he could remember, recorded two points from the lecture on romantic love and noted that in both Auden kept close to de Rougemont. The first is that romantic lovers are narcissists, who keep a heroic picture of themselves as unlike anyone else. The rest of the world tries to correct that picture, and two such people who fall in love confirm it for each other. The second is that passion needs an obstacle, because desire grows stronger when it is blocked. Where the world supplies none, the lovers must make one, as Tristan and Iseult (Wagner’s Isolde) do in the old story when they sleep with a drawn sword between them. The obstacle such lovers really need, Auden said, is one that cannot be overcome, so that only death can unite them. He told the class that Wagner understood the psychology of romantic love perfectly.

In “Balaam and His Ass,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden calls it fortunate that Wagner made an opera of the story. A reader of the medieval legend, he says, imagines a prince and a princess of perfect beauty, while an audience at the opera sees “a Wagnerian tenor and soprano in all their corseted bulk.” The audience is saved in this way from supposing that the lovers’ passion has anything to do with looks. Auden argues that beauty is something time takes away, and that a passion which admits no change cannot come from a quality of that kind. He takes the love potion to mean, among other things, that each of the lovers cares so little who the other is that chance might as well have paired them.

Auden thinks it fortunate too that an opera cannot show the lovers consummating their love. Whatever Wagner intended by the duet in the second act, what the audience sees is two people singing of their desire, and the consummation is always about to come and never does. Auden holds that what the stage shows is the truth about these two, because each of them declares a boundless willingness to give everything and in practice holds back. If they yielded, each would learn what the other is like, and the passion would turn into something else. What each of them wants is not the other person but something to be reached by means of the other, which he calls Nirvana, the unity there was before there were separate persons.

Auden ends with the servants, Brangäne and Kurwenal, as he ends his account of *Don Giovanni* (week 6) with Leporello. He points out four turns of the plot, each of them the work of one of the two. Kurwenal’s mockery, for example, makes Isolde angry enough to decide on poison, and Brangäne puts the love potion in its place. Auden then imagines the two servants in real life as an ordinary married couple in a dingy suburban house, short of money, with more children than is usual. Let those two daydream of ideal love, he says, and what they dream will come close to Tristan and Isolde’s passion, in a world without children, jobs or food. But the dreamers are sane and cannot keep their sense of reality out of the dream, and that is why the lovers in it are doomed.
sources: Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” pp. 135–139.
“Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 120–123.

questions.text: The Button-moulder tells Peer that he has never been himself. What would Peer have had to do to be himself?
gloss: The trolls have one motto and humans another; both are given in Act 2, Scene 6. The Button-moulder comes for Peer in Act 5, Scene 7, and in Scene 9 explains what he means by being oneself.

paras: Auden wrote about *Peer Gynt* in “Genius & Apostle,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). He finds that the whole play asks one question, what a person’s real self is, and answers it in several ways. An animal is itself without having to ask. Auden names two ways of living in which a human being comes near to that. The nearer is the second nature people take from heredity and custom. The other is a life governed by one overriding personal interest, like that of the peasant in the play who cuts off a finger to escape conscription. Neither satisfies Peer. He tells his mother that he will be an emperor, and Auden remarks that the only empire safe from everyone else is a person’s own consciousness.

Auden observes that the Peer of the play has no appetites of the ordinary kind and only plays at having them. He explains that Ibsen wanted a poet for a hero and knew that a poet cannot be put on the stage directly, because the making of a poem is work, and work cannot be acted. Ibsen’s solution, Auden says, is to show “a man who treats nearly everything he does as a role,” so that play-acting stands on the stage for the writing of poems. A real poet would have written one play about a slave trader and another about a prophet, whereas Peer plays at being each.

According to the essay, a poet is like a dreamer or a madman, except that those two are in earnest about what they imagine. Poets pretend for fun and know that they are pretending. So Peer will swear to the troll king that a cow is a beautiful girl, and will not have the operation on his eyes that would stop him from telling the difference.

The play gives humans the motto to be oneself, and gives trolls the motto to be enough for oneself. Ibsen has made his poet an actor, and Auden argues that people whose calling is to act can be true to themselves only by pretending to be someone else. When Peer asks at the end where his real self has been, Solveig says it has been in her faith, her hope and her love. Auden says that Ibsen leaves it in doubt whether she is right, and that the price of the poet’s calling may after all be the Button-moulder’s ladle, where Peer would be melted down.

Auden calls the play fascinating but says that its structure is not satisfying. In his account a prologue and an epilogue make up almost the whole play and contain nearly all its best scenes. The prologue is about how a boy is marked out to be a poet, and the epilogue about how an old poet answers for his life when death is near. Only the fourth act shows the grown poet at work, and Auden finds the number of its scenes and characters arbitrary.
sources: “Genius & Apostle,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 435–441.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about third sons in fairy tales
paras: Donald Pearce, a student in the class, recalled that when he asked to join the course, one of the questions Auden put to him was whether he had read many fairy tales. During the weeks on Shakespeare, Auden sent the class home with the order “Read lots of fairy stories over the weekend!” No record has been found of what Auden made of *The Brothers Karamazov* in class, but in his introduction to *Tales of Grimm and Andersen* (1952) he examines one tale about a third son.

In “The Water of Life” a king is sick, and his three sons go out in turn to look for the water that will cure him. On the road a dwarf asks each of them where he is going. Both elder brothers answer him rudely and are shut up in ravines, and the youngest answers politely and is told where the water is.

The hero of such a tale, Auden says, begins obscure or despised, and in this one he stands in the third or lowest place. He passes a test that his brothers fail. In Auden’s account the brothers pay the dwarf no attention because he seems the least likely of helpers, because they are impatient and have nothing in mind but their own success, and because they trust too much in their own powers and want their father’s reward without loving him. The hero is humble enough to ask for help, cares whether his father recovers, and is well disposed toward everyone.

The tale suggests to Auden that people are seldom strong where they pride themselves on their strength, and are often strong in what they think unimportant or count as a weakness. Nobody succeeds by will alone, because success takes luck as well. Auden gives luck a second name, grace, and says that it is never withheld from those who ask humbly.

Auden was writing about the hero of a fairy tale, and the application to Alyosha is this site’s. In your reply, take the three qualities Auden finds in the hero: the humility to ask for help, concern for his father’s recovery, and good will toward everyone. Say which of them Alyosha has shown by the end of Book III, and compare that with what you wrote in your paper.
sources: “Grimm and Andersen,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 201–203.
Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” pp. 133 and 144, for the fairy tales.

making.title: Every sentence a lie
making.short: A story or an essay with a lie in every sentence
brief: In May 1939 Auden taught for four weeks at St. Mark’s School in Massachusetts. One of the boys remembered that the first thing Auden assigned the class was a story or an essay with a lie in each sentence.

Writing about *Peer Gynt*, Auden says that the poet “asserts his freedom by lying,” and explains that he means the making of worlds the poet knows to be imaginary. This exercise asks you to do the same on a small scale.
rules: Write a story or an essay of twelve to twenty sentences. Put each sentence on a line of its own.
Take a subject you know: your own day, your street, your family, your work.
Every sentence must contain a lie, a statement about that subject which you know to be false.
The whole piece must be consistent with itself, so that a stranger would believe all of it.
making.reflect: Which sentence came out true in spite of you? If none did, which lie was hardest to keep up?

paras: *Carmen* runs a little over two and a half hours. At the first performance, in Paris in March 1875, the scenes between the musical numbers (the songs, duets and choruses) were spoken. The English printed here follows the version made for Vienna that fall by Ernest Guiraud, a composer and a friend of Bizet’s, in which those scenes are shortened and sung. If your recording has the spoken scenes, you will hear more than you read.
While you listen, notice what Carmen offers Don José in the second act, and what he must give up to take it.

The words are by Henri Meilhac and Ludovic Halévy, from a story by Prosper Mérimée. Bizet died three months after the first performance. Auden assigned this libretto, with that of *Tristan* (the opera for week 7), as reading for his lectures on love in the fall of 1941.

In “Balaam and His Ass,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden compares the lovers in *Tristan* with the lovers in *Carmen*. The passion of Tristan and Isolde is equal on both sides, and he says that nobody meets such a pair in life. What does occur in life is the one-sided kind, as with Don José and Carmen, where one party adores and the other plays the Cruel Fair, the beauty who will not love in return.

Auden reasons that idolatry runs only one way. “My idol,” he writes, “is that which I make responsible for my existence in order that I may have no responsibility for myself.” If the idol demanded responsibility in return, it would stop being one.

Carmen’s offer to Don José, the one you were asked to notice, is quoted in *The Enchafèd Flood*, the lectures Auden gave in 1949 on the sea in Romantic writing. In those lectures Auden says that the Romantics treated the sea and the desert alike as wilderness, places with no community, where a person is free of both the evils and the duties of life among others. He cites Jules Verne’s Captain Nemo, who commands a submarine and says that below the surface of the sea no ruler’s power can reach him. Auden then writes, “And so Carmen tempts Don José to leave the fertile plain for the barren lawless mountains,” where José would depend on nobody and have no officer to obey.
On the next page Auden says that such a place has a cost, because it is lonely as well as free, and whoever is there, by choice or by fate, will at times long for home and company.

auden.title: What Auden wrote in 1939
paras: In the summer of 1939 Auden wrote most of a book in prose, *The Prolific and the Devourer*. He did not finish it, and it was printed only after his death. One part of it treats the three temptations of Jesus by Satan in the wilderness. In the third, as Auden tells it, Satan argues that people love no one but themselves, so that the way to live is to be stronger than the next person. Auden says that the evidence for Satan’s case can be found in many books, among them Plato’s *Republic*, Machiavelli’s *The Prince*, Hobbes’s *Leviathan* and Hitler’s *Mein Kampf*, but that the case is “nowhere perhaps more completely and cogently expressed” than by the Grand Inquisitor.

Auden observes that Jesus gives the Inquisitor no answer, as he gave none to Satan or to Pilate. In Auden’s view Jesus has no need to answer, because all three are answered by what they have themselves lived through: they know what they are doing, and they know that they have failed.

Auden then writes out the reply that the Prisoner does not give. He supposes that Jesus hears the case not from the Inquisitor but from an attendant who only repeats what his master has said. The reply is spoken to that attendant and answers three of the Inquisitor’s sentences in turn.

The first is that nothing has ever been harder for people to bear than freedom. The reply grants that freedom is what Jesus offers. It sets aside the kind in which a person could as well do one thing as another and nothing matters more than anything else, and names the freedom to know the truth. The Inquisitor claims to offer the same freedom. Jesus says to the attendant, “The difference between us is that, while he professes to tell you what that truth is, I know that I cannot tell you.” He adds that he can only say how to look for it, and that the truth is within each person.

The second is that the craving to worship in common has been the chief misery of each person and of humankind from the beginning. Worship, the reply says, is a state of love, and people meet in it all the time without holding the same beliefs: lovers, a family at a reunion, a gang of workmen on a job. That is why the act chosen for common worship was a meal, which anyone can share. Jesus says that it is the Inquisitor who has made a mystery of that meal, and he continues, “I tell you that even a Rotary Club dinner is nearer my intention than the Mass.”

The third is the Inquisitor’s boast that the Church has corrected the Prisoner’s work and founded it on “miracle, mystery and authority.” The reply says that a miracle is an event that human knowledge was too poor to predict, and that it has done its work when it is understood and can be repeated. On mystery the reply has only its earlier remark about the meal. The only authority that people cannot disobey, it says, is their own idea of the truth. It ends with Jesus saying that any words of his that human experience contradicted would be false, whoever he claimed to be.

The year after writing this speech, Auden went back to the Anglican church in which he had been brought up, and he stayed in it for the rest of his life. In your reply, say whether Dostoevsky’s Prisoner could have made the speech Auden wrote, and whether the kiss says anything that the speech does not.
sources: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 48–58.
Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden* (Princeton University Press, 2017), p. 471, for Auden’s return to the church.

auden.title: What Auden said elsewhere
paras: Nothing by Auden about “Rebellion,” the chapter in which Ivan returns his ticket, has been found. This site brings in two remarks Auden made on other occasions, one in the classroom in 1941 and one in an introduction he published in 1952, and applies them to Ivan.

The first is from the opening meeting of Auden’s course. He began by reading the class a list of definitions, “so that we shall have some ground in common.” Donald Pearce, a student in the class who wrote down after lectures what he could remember, preserved six of them. One of the six is “I believe in order that I may understand; never the reverse.” Ivan tells Alyosha that he accepts God but cannot accept the world God made. He also says that he has a Euclidean mind and wants to see justice done with his own eyes. By asking to see justice before he accepts the world, he does the reverse of what the definition requires.

The second is from the introduction Auden wrote to a selection from Søren Kierkegaard, whose *Fear and Trembling* you read in week 6. In that introduction he says that Kierkegaard, like Pascal (the *Pensées*, weeks 5 and 6), was marked out by fate as an exception who would suffer no matter what he did. People who suffer by fate are tempted in ways of their own. Those who look only at their own case are drawn to conclude that God is cruel and takes pleasure in the pain of the innocent, and Auden calls that conclusion demonic defiance. Those who begin by holding that God is good are drawn to conclude that they must be guilty of something, though they cannot tell what, and he calls that demonic despair.

Ivan’s case resembles demonic defiance, though it differs because the suffering he brings in evidence is not his own. In your reply, say whether that difference makes his refusal stronger or weaker. Keep demonic despair in mind for the last novel on the list, *The Castle*.
sources: Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” pp. 131–132.
“Søren Kierkegaard,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 169.

paras: *La Traviata* runs a little over two hours. The English translation printed here calls the opera *The Lost One*.
The words are by Francesco Maria Piave, from a play by the younger Alexandre Dumas, *La Dame aux camélias*. The opera was first performed in Venice in March 1853.

In the last act Germont, Alfred’s father, comes into the room where Violetta, the woman Alfred loves, is dying. Listen for that moment, which in the libretto is the beginning of the last scene of Act 3, and notice what the orchestra plays as Germont enters. Alfred is Alfredo in the Italian that is sung.

In “Notes on Music and Opera,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden says that all drama rests on a mistake. Someone takes an enemy for a friend, or a young nobleman in disguise for a chambermaid. First the mistake is made, and then it is found out. According to the essay, a playwright can also show people deceiving themselves, but a librettist cannot, because music is direct and does not reflect on what it says: “whatever is sung is the case.” The most that can be done is to hint at self-deception by setting the orchestra against the singer. Auden cites “the jolly tripping notes” that accompany Germont to Violetta’s deathbed at the moment you were asked to listen for, but he adds that such devices confuse the listener unless they are used very rarely.

In the same essay Auden says that opera imitates human willfulness, the way people insist on having their feelings, whatever the cost to themselves. So opera cannot show the kind of character a novel shows, a person who could turn out good or bad and who is acted on as well as acting. Each of the great roles, he says, is “a passionate and willful state of being,” and in real life all of them would be bores.

Auden says that a libretto, unlike a play, has no need to be probable. A good one is a melodrama, which puts its characters in situations so tragic or so fantastic that speech would not be enough for them. “No good opera plot can be sensible,” he writes, “for people do not sing when they are feeling sensible.” Compare what Auden says of opera with this week’s novel, in which the characters talk for whole chapters and several of them deceive themselves. The comparison is this site’s and not Auden’s, and you are not asked to write anything about it.
sources: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 470–472.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about murder stories
paras: In 1948 Auden published “The Guilty Vicarage,” an essay on detective stories, and he reprinted it in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). The essay begins with his own reading of such stories, which he calls an addiction of the same kind as tobacco or alcohol. It then accepts the common definition of a detective story as a story that asks who did the murder, and you have just written on whether *The Brothers Karamazov* asks the same thing. Auden argues that murder is unlike every other crime, because a thief can give back what was stolen and the victim of a rape can forgive, but murder does away with the person it wrongs. Society then has to act for the victim, and it is society that must exact a penalty or forgive.

A detective story, as he describes it, needs a closed society, so that the murderer cannot be an outsider. A family is one of his examples. The society must also seem innocent. The murder shows that one member is no longer innocent, and until the murderer is found everyone is a suspect and has to answer to the law. Then a detective from outside names the guilty one, who is taken away, and all the rest are innocent again. Auden calls this sequence a magic formula. It gives the reader the illusion of having nothing to do with the murderer, and for that reason he counts such books as escape literature and not as works of art.

According to the essay, a work of art about a murder compels the reader to identify with the murderer, an identification the reader would rather not admit. Auden names another novel by Dostoevsky, *Crime and Punishment*, as an example. A detective story gives its reader what Auden calls a fantasy, and he writes, “The identification of fantasy is always an attempt to avoid one’s own suffering: the identification of art is a sharing in the suffering of another.”

This site tries the formula on *The Brothers Karamazov*, which the essay does not mention. The novel has the closed family and the murdered father, and at the end of Book IX the officers take Mitya away. In your reply, say whether that leaves the rest of the family innocent again, as it would in a detective story.
sources: “The Guilty Vicarage,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 146–147, 149–150 and 158.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about guilt
paras: In 1948 Auden published “The Guilty Vicarage,” an essay on detective stories, and he reprinted it in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). At the head of the essay he put a verse from Saint Paul’s letter to the Romans (7:7), which says that a person would not know what sin is without the law: “I had not known sin, but by the law.” Further on Auden confesses to the kind of guilt the question asks about. To some degree he can refuse to act on the desires that tempt him, he says, but he cannot keep from having them, and having them makes him feel guilty.

He describes himself as a person with a sense of sin, which he distinguishes from ethics. Ethics deals with desires and acts, and tells a person to choose the good ones and reject the bad. The sense of sin is guilt at having a choice to make at all, and however good a person becomes, Auden says, that guilt is the same as it was.

Auden suspects that a typical reader of detective stories suffers from the same guilt. The reader’s daydream is of being put back in the Garden of Eden, with the guilt carried off by somebody else. As this site reads the novel, Mitya could take what the daydream offers. He says that he did not strike the blow, and if he did not, he could leave the guilt to whoever did. Notice that he turns the offer down, and that he accepts the punishment for what he meant to do.
sources: “The Guilty Vicarage,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 146 and 157–158.

*A Season in Hell*, which the reading list calls by its French title, *Une Saison en Enfer*, is under 25 pages. Arthur Rimbaud, a French poet, wrote it at eighteen and had it printed the same year, 1873. The translation here appeared in *The Dial*, an American magazine, in 1920. The translator left the poems of one chapter in French, and this week’s exercise is to translate one of them.

paras: *Fidelio*, Beethoven’s only opera, runs about two hours.

The second act has two settings, a dungeon and the parade ground of the castle, and many performances play an overture, known as *Leonore* No. 3, between them. Beethoven wrote that overture for the version of 1806, and it is not part of the opera as he left it in 1814. In the libretto printed here, which numbers a new scene whenever someone enters or leaves, the second setting begins at Scene 7 and is called a hall in the castle. If the performance you hear has the overture, notice what happens to the drama while it is being played.

The words are by Joseph Sonnleithner, who worked from a French libretto by Jean-Nicolas Bouilly, and Georg Friedrich Treitschke revised them later. The opera was first performed in Vienna in 1805, and the form now played dates from 1814. The arias and ensembles are sung in German, and the dialogue between them is spoken.

In “Notes on Music and Opera,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden writes, “In opera the orchestra is addressed to the singers, not to the audience.” An opera-lover puts up with an orchestral interlude, and even enjoys it, on condition that it is filling in time while tired singers rest or the set is changed, and counts any other playing by the orchestra alone as time wasted. Auden grants that *Leonore* No. 3 is a fine piece in the concert hall, but says that when it is played in the opera house between the two settings of the second act, “it becomes twelve minutes of acute boredom.”

On the next page Auden says that the words of a libretto are not addressed to the public either, and calls them “a private letter to the composer.” Their one great moment is when they put a melody into the composer’s head, and after that they must get out of the way and not mind what is done with them.
sources: “Notes on Music and Opera,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 472–473.
