auden.title: What Auden wrote about the devil
paras: Auden gave the question in 1942–43, his first year at Swarthmore College, in a course on Elizabethan literature, and no answer of his has been found. The subject of that course points to the devil in Marlowe’s play *Doctor Faustus*. Putting the question to Ivan’s visitor is this site’s choice.

In the spring of 1941, a few months before the Michigan course began, Auden published *New Year Letter*, a long poem with notes. Much of its second part is about the Devil, whom the poem calls Mephistopheles. What he offers people, the poem says, are half-truths, and he is lost if anyone asks him to say exactly what he thinks. One of the notes says, “The Devil, indeed, is the father of Poetry, for poetry might be defined as the clear expression of mixed feelings.”

In “Balaam and His Ass,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden says that the Devil changes his shape with the age. In ages when people were tempted to take some finite thing for the holy itself, the Devil appeared as a finite thing, such as a beautiful woman or a bag of gold. According to the essay, Auden’s own age tires of each idol and takes up the next so quickly that none can properly be called an idol, and its real idolatry, the one that lasts, is of possibility. The Devil appears to such an age as Mephisto, the devil in Goethe’s *Faust*, that is, as an actor, and actors have no name of their own because they bear so many. Auden calls Mephisto “the manifestation of possibility without actuality,” and describes Faust as a man who will not be anyone in particular and wants only to turn into someone else. The two are so nearly one, in his account, that he would have them played by identical twins.

The comparison that follows is this site’s and not Auden’s. Ivan calls the visitor one side of himself, the nastiest and stupidest, which makes the two as nearly one as Faust and Mephisto are in Auden’s account. In the same chapter, Book XI, Chapter 9, the visitor says what he dreams of becoming. In your reply, say whether that dream fits Auden’s phrase for Mephisto, “possibility without actuality,” and whether it explains why this devil is sad.

auden.title: What Auden required, and what was said of it
paras: Nothing by Auden about Alyosha’s speech at the stone has been found, nor has any essay of his in defense of memorizing, so what he thought of it has to be judged from what he required of his classes and from a few remarks of his own.

Dorothy Farnan, a graduate student at Michigan in 1941, was not in the class, and in *Auden in Love*, her book of 1984, she reports what she heard from those who were. By her account Auden held memory work to be a first-rate training for the mind. Using his first name, she writes that “Wystan insisted that his students memorize or fail, and memorize they did.”

In “The Poet & the City,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden imagines a college for poets in which the students learn thousands of lines of verse by heart, in several languages. In an interview given near the end of his life and printed in 1974, he was asked whether he had ever taught writing. He said that he never had, and that if he had to teach poetry he would keep to learning poems by heart and to prosody, rhetoric and philology. He allowed that he might be wrong, but he could see nothing to be learned in such a class except technical things.

More than forty years after the course, Donald Pearce, a student in the class who wrote down after lectures what he could remember, reported that the class had resisted when the examination was announced. The first canto took him a week of afternoons, a canto a few weeks later took him three afternoons, and he learned the last in one. At the examination, which ended the first semester, he wrote out the five cantos, and he calls the feat “possibly the most valuable thing I learned from W. H. Auden.” He has been grateful for it ever since, he says, and has sometimes asked classes of his own to attempt feats like it, with the same resistance at first and a similar gratitude in the end.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about Rimbaud
paras: Rimbaud gave up writing at about twenty and spent most of the rest of his life as a trader in Arabia and East Africa. Reviewing a biography of him in 1939, Auden wrote that as a man of action Rimbaud “was a self-tortured failure, for no one can live by will alone.”

Ten years later Auden discussed Rimbaud at the end of *The Enchafèd Flood*, which prints three lectures he gave at the University of Virginia in 1949 on the sea in Romantic writing. He says in those lectures that from about 1770 to 1914 the great heroes were not men of action but artists and scientists, and that artists became the heroes of their own epics. He takes Faust, Don Juan and Captain Ahab of *Moby-Dick* (week 11) to be figures in which their authors imagined themselves, and not the true heroes of their books. Such a figure acts less for the sake of the deed than to find out what acting feels like. Artists who worked in this way, he says, experimented on themselves and kept the record, and they knew excitements and terrors that had hardly been known before. He quotes the page of “Alchemy of the Word” on hallucination, and says that what Rimbaud reports of himself there holds, more or less, for every one of them.

Auden finds it more remarkable that some of these artists saw through the idea of the artist as hero. They came to see that artists were not the religious heroes they had taken themselves for, but only explorers of possibility, like Ishmael, who tells the story of *Moby-Dick*. Auden pictures the Button-moulder of *Peer Gynt* (week 7) waiting for such artists at the next crossroads, to ask them whether they have become their actual selves. As instances he quotes a passage of *Moby-Dick* and the passage of “Adieu” in which Rimbaud, who had called himself a wizard or an angel, is brought back to earth and calls himself a peasant.

In “Making, Knowing and Judging,” a lecture of 1956 printed in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden writes of the Rimbaud Myth, as he calls the story of a great poet who stops writing by choice and not for lack of anything more to say. He says that it “may not be true, I am pretty sure it is not, but as a myth it haunts the artistic conscience of this century.”
sources: “Heretics,” a review of 1939, quoted in Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden*, pp. 348–349.

brief: At Michigan Auden had each student translate a poem from German, French or Latin. Students picked a language they had not studied and were allowed no help but a dictionary. This site assigns all three translations, and in each a word list takes the place of the dictionary. The Latin was in week 2, this is the French, and the German is in week 14.

In “Alchemy of the Word” Rimbaud quotes several of his own poems, and the translator of 1920 left them all in French. The poem for this exercise is the one that follows the paragraph in which Rimbaud says that he stripped the azure from the sky.
rules: Make an English poem of it, in twenty-four short lines, rhymed or unrhymed as you choose.

Work from the word list alone, with no dictionary and no published translation. You may use English words that are not in the list. No line of the French has more than five syllables, so keep each of your lines short.
One word in line 14 is Latin. Decide what to do with it.
If you have studied French, do this exercise anyway, and spend more time on the German in week 14.

questions.text: Ishmael was brought up a Presbyterian. In Chapter 10 he joins Queequeg in the worship of a wooden idol, and he reasons his way to it in one paragraph. Is the reasoning sound?
gloss: Chapter 10, “A Bosom Friend.” Then see what Queequeg does on the boat to Nantucket in Chapter 13.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about Ishmael’s road to the ship
paras: In *The Enchafèd Flood*, the book of his 1949 lectures on the sea in Romantic writing, Auden reads everything before the Pequod sails as a set of tests. Ishmael has made up his mind to go to sea, but he has not signed, and at each step he could still turn around and go back to the city. The first test is a fright: he pushes open the door of what he takes for an inn and finds a church, with a sermon on hell in progress. The last are Elijah’s warning on the wharf and the interview with the two Quaker owners.

The longest test is Queequeg. Ishmael starts with two fixed notions, which Auden says readers of *Moby-Dick* share: that people who are not white must be ugly, and that pagans cannot keep the commandment to love their neighbor, since they have never been given it. He loses both through Queequeg, who left his island to learn the truth from Christians, found that the people who know it do not obey it, and settled down to live as a pagan among them. On the boat to Nantucket Queequeg saves the life of a man who has just insulted him. Auden says that in doing so he shows a Christian’s forgiveness and love without any effort, and calls him “a doer of the Word who has never heard the Word.”

According to Auden, Ishmael accepts Queequeg by taking part in his worship of the idol, and the acceptance proves Ishmael fit for the voyage. No comment by Auden on Ishmael’s paragraph of reasoning has been found.

Auden says that for Ishmael, and for the reader who travels with him, the voyage is an exploration. Ishmael comes through it unchanged except in what he knows of himself and of other people. He had to be tested beforehand, Auden says, to find out whether he was fit for an exploration of that kind, and after passing the tests he has nothing left to do but record. The rest of the crew, by contrast, gain no knowledge of themselves, and the voyage changes them as the reader watches.
sources: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 113–115 and 119.

questions.text: Father Mapple says near the start of his sermon on the Book of Jonah that to obey God we must disobey ourselves. At the end he says that delight belongs to whoever stands forth “his own inexorable self.” Can one person do both?
gloss: Chapter 9. Father Mapple speaks of obeying God at the end of the first long paragraph of his sermon, just before he begins the story of Jonah. He speaks of delight in the last paragraph of the sermon, which is the next-to-last paragraph of the chapter.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about the sermon
paras: Auden says in *The Enchafèd Flood*, the book of his 1949 lectures on the sea in Romantic writing, that Father Mapple’s sermon has sometimes been called splendid and beside the point, but that it is “an essential clue to the meaning of the whole book.” Melville put it early, before the Pequod sails, so that readers would have a standard for judging what Ahab and the others say and do afterward.

Jonah, as Auden retells the story, knows the Word of God and is called to do more than know it: he is to act on it with his whole passion, as a religious hero. He runs away out of pride, afraid that nobody will listen to him or admire him. His punishment is to be faced with what is really great, a storm and a whale, next to which the greatest emperor is puny. Inside the whale he loses his one gift, the power to hear the Word. He repents instead of despairing and trusts the God he cannot hear, and he is forgiven and put ashore to do what he was told.

Auden says that Father Mapple’s two statements only appear to contradict each other, and that they say what the Button-moulder says to Peer in Ibsen’s *Peer Gynt*, the play you read in week 7. The Button-moulder, who has come to melt Peer down, tells him that being oneself means slaying oneself. He doubts that Peer will understand this, so he puts it another way: it means carrying out the Master’s intention in everything.

Auden then distinguishes the ego from the self, which together make a person. The self is what a person has been given. It has powers it does not know of, it can begin nothing, and it wants only to stay as it is, content with itself and in need of nothing. The ego is the part that decides. Auden says that it can go wrong in three ways: first, by refusing to look honestly at the self it has; second, by preferring a false god, one it thinks it can manage, to the true God; third, by knowing the self and what is required of it and still disobeying, out of weakness or out of defiance. Keep the third way in mind for Ahab, and defiance above all. In this passage Auden does not apply the distinction to Father Mapple’s two statements, so in your reply say of each statement whether the self it speaks of is the self a person has been given or the ego that decides.
sources: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 116–119.

questions.text: Ahab lost his leg before the book begins. Chapter 41 says what he made of the loss. What else could he have made of it?
gloss: Chapter 41, “Moby Dick.” Then go back to Chapter 36 and read what Starbuck says to Ahab on the quarter-deck, and what Ahab answers.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about Ahab
paras: In December 1945 Auden wrote about *Moby-Dick* on the front page of *The New York Times Book Review*, under the title “The Christian Tragic Hero.” He begins by calling Greek tragedy the tragedy of necessity, which leaves the spectator sorry that things had to happen as they did. In Christian tragedy, which he calls the tragedy of possibility, the spectator thinks, “What a pity it was this way when it might have been otherwise.” By Christian he means that an author’s idea of what a person is derives from Christian doctrine, whether or not the author believed it.

Auden says that a Greek hero begins exceptionally fortunate and ends ruined, and that Ahab starts where the Greek hero finishes, as a man marked out by misfortune. A Greek audience would have had to take the lost leg as a punishment for sin. For Ahab, Auden says, it is a temptation and “an opportunity to choose.” Ahab chooses wrongly and keeps to his choice, and in doing so he punishes himself.

In *The Enchafèd Flood*, the book of his 1949 lectures on the sea in Romantic writing, Auden asks what the loss of the leg was telling Ahab to become. The question, he says, can be answered only in the negative: “At least, not to go on whaling.” He guesses that the loss told Ahab to stop being someone set apart from other people by his abilities, and to become a happy husband and father or a monk. Auden notes that Ahab does not call his punishment just and does not declare, as Job does in the Bible, that he will trust the one who slays him. Auden has him say instead, “Thou art guilty and shalt be punished,” without naming the one addressed.

Auden says that nothing in Ahab’s nature wants to go chasing a whale around the world, old and maimed as he is, and that by Ahab’s own admission what it wants is peace, a family and happiness. It is as if Ahab, knowing that God wanted these things for him too, willed for that reason to be miserable at every moment. Auden calls him a representation of defiant despair, “perhaps the greatest in literature.”
sources: “The Christian Tragic Hero,” *The New York Times Book Review*, December 16, 1945, reprinted in *Prose, Volume II*, pp. 258–261.
*The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 134–137.

brief: In the spring of 1942 Auden gave a second course at Michigan, English 136, on the analysis of poetry. The first part of its final examination, on May 21, was on Milton’s “Lycidas,” which the class had been made to look up word by word (see week 4). One question printed the last eight lines of the poem with about a dozen words changed. The whole instruction was “Emend the following.”

You cannot finish until you have marked at least seven words and written a correction for each. Ten words were changed, so if you are sure of fewer than seven, mark the ones you most suspect until you have seven. The page shows which of your corrections were right only after you finish.
The page lists with your result every unchanged word that you marked and corrected, so once you have seven, mark another word only if you believe it has been changed.

units.title: *Moby-Dick*: the whale
intro: This week you read the middle of the book, about two hundred pages. Little happens to Ahab in it. The Pequod lowers her boats after whales and meets four ships, and Ishmael describes the sperm whale part by part, from the head to the tail.

Do not skip the chapters on rope, blubber, heads and tails. The first question is about two of them, and the exercise asks you to write a chapter of that kind yourself, on the model of Chapter 32, which you have already read.
Wagner’s opera *The Flying Dutchman* is also assigned this week. *Purgatorio* XXVIII is due at the end of the week.

paras: The opera runs about two hours and a quarter, and is often played without a break.

Wagner wrote the words himself, as he did for all his operas. He took the story from the German poet Heinrich Heine. The opera was first performed in Dresden in January 1843, and it is sung in German.
While you listen, notice how much Senta, a Norwegian sea captain’s daughter, knows about the Dutchman before he comes through the door, and where she learned it.

auden.title: What Auden wrote that bears on this opera
paras: Auden names the hero of this opera only in passing, as a type, and no account by him of the opera itself has been found. In *The Enchafèd Flood*, the book of his 1949 lectures on the sea in Romantic writing, he describes the hero of the Romantics as having two natures. Half of him is an exile, and Auden gives the exile three names: the Ishmael of Genesis, the Wandering Jew (the man of legend who must walk the earth until the end of the world) and the Flying Dutchman. The other half is Don Quixote, the man with a mission.

The Dutchman is doomed by an oath. Senta tells the story in her ballad: he swore that he would round a cape if he had to sail forever, and he was taken at his word. Auden has a page on oaths in his account of Ahab, who makes his harpooneers swear to hunt the White Whale to the death. An oath, he says, commits a person’s future. It is right to swear to a direction of the will, as a man does who vows at the altar to love his wife until death, but wrong to swear to a particular act. For the wrong kind Auden imagines a husband’s vow to give his wife a pound of candy a week, when she may get diabetes. As this site applies the rule, the Dutchman’s oath to round one cape was an oath to a particular act, and Senta’s last words, a vow to be his until death, are an oath to a direction of the will.

In the notes to *New Year Letter*, his long poem of 1941, Auden says that Wagner, in expressing the sufferings of failure, is “perhaps the greatest genius who ever lived,” but that happiness and success were beyond him. For friendship and for love that is returned, a listener has to go to Mozart. The poem itself sums up a Wagner plot in a couplet: “And Woman, passive as in dreams, / Redeems, redeems, redeems, redeems.”

In a review of 1969 Auden calls the German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche by far the best guide to Wagner. Nietzsche’s *The Case of Wagner* is one of the books of criticism recommended on the reading list. The passage Auden quotes from him says that somebody in a Wagner opera always wants to be saved. Of *The Flying Dutchman* it says that even the Wandering Jew, as Nietzsche calls the Dutchman, is saved and settles down once he marries.

*New Year Letter* (Faber and Faber, 1941), Part III, and the note to line 1432.

questions.text: Chapter 60 is about rope and Chapter 68 is about blubber. Each ends by turning to the reader. Take one of them and say how Melville gets from the fact about whaling to the lesson. Does the lesson follow from the fact, or is it laid on top of it?

auden.title: What Auden wrote about the three kinds of meaning in the book
paras: Auden says in *The Enchafèd Flood*, the book of his 1949 lectures on the sea in Romantic writing, that *Moby-Dick* has meaning of three kinds. The first kind is the figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole. Leave out the White Whale, he says, and the book is one large figure of that sort: Melville takes whaling, a trade he had worked at, and makes it stand for anybody’s life. Whalemen live by killing, and so does everyone in one way or another. The owners of the Pequod are Quakers, who profess never to shed blood, and they see nothing odd in their business. Each of the mates shows what he is by how he goes about killing whales. For this kind of meaning, Auden adds, another trade would have done as well, so long as Melville knew it.

The second kind is parable, where something in one part of life is made to answer, point for point, to something in another. As examples Auden quotes the two endings the question asked about, the whale-lines that everyone lives in and the whale that keeps its own temperature at the Equator and at the Pole. The nine ships that the Pequod meets, which you will chart next week, are a third example. Auden says that the method is deliberate, that it is the one that the Church Fathers, the Christian writers of the first centuries, used when they interpreted Scripture, and that the reader grasps each correspondence by reasoning.

The third kind is symbol in the true sense, and, according to Auden, Melville uses it when he writes about the White Whale. By a symbol Auden means something that is felt to matter before anyone can say why, and in which different people see different things. The other question this week is about what the whale is to Ahab and to Ishmael.

Charles Miller took the course in the fall of 1941 and lived in Auden’s house at the time. He remembered that Auden never discussed Melville but said many times that *Moby-Dick* “is really an epic poem, and should be read that way.” In Miller’s view Auden was inclined to revere Melville and not to examine him. This site adds that an epic stops for lists and for gear, as Homer’s *Iliad* stops for its catalog of ships and for the shield of Achilles.
sources: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 58–62.
Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (Scribner, 1983), p. 135.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about the whale
paras: In *The Enchafèd Flood*, the book of his 1949 lectures on the sea in Romantic writing, Auden defines a symbol as something felt to matter before anyone can say why. A symbol, he says, never has a single meaning, and different people see different things in it. In this a symbol is unlike a parable, in which one thing answers to one thing. Auden quotes as examples of parable the lessons Melville draws at the end of Chapters 60 and 68.

To Ahab, in the words Auden quotes from the speech on the quarter-deck, the whale is a mask, and in it he sees great strength driven by malice. To Gabriel, the madman of the Jeroboam, it has similar qualities, but Gabriel worships it. Steelkilt of the Town-Ho meets in it God’s justice and mercy: it kills the man he was about to murder, and so keeps him from murder. To Starbuck it means death, or his own fatal tie to his captain. Ishmael, whom Auden does not separate from Melville, finds it neither good nor evil. To him, Auden says, it is “numinous”: the whale shows him a divine power and majesty beyond any human measure of right and wrong.

In February of 1941, the year of the course, Auden reviewed three books by Franz Kafka, among them *The Castle*, which you will read in weeks 14 and 15. He made the review into an essay on quest stories, from the old tales of the Holy Grail to Kafka. A footnote to the essay calls *Moby-Dick*, among such stories, “a unique exception.” Nobody in the book, Auden says, is looking for salvation, and the whale is two figures of the old stories in one, the sacred thing that is sought and the monster that guards it.

That spring Auden published *New Year Letter*, his long poem with notes. One of the notes says that most American novels are parables, in which the struggle takes place inside a person, and that “Melville’s sea is not a real sea nor his whale a real whale.” Eight years later, in *The Enchafèd Flood*, Auden uses the word parable more narrowly, for the lessons Melville draws from whaling, and calls the whale a symbol.

making.title: A chapter in the manner of “Cetology”
making.short: A parody: sort something you know as Melville sorts the whales
brief: In “The Poet & the City,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), Auden imagines a college for poets. The library has no criticism on its shelves, and the students practice criticism in one way only, by writing parodies. This is the second parody of the course, after the parody of Blake’s Proverbs of Hell in week 6.

Some chapters of *Moby-Dick* pretend to be treatises. “Cetology” (Chapter 32) sorts the whales by size into three Books named after the sizes of printed books, Folio, Octavo and Duodecimo, and gives each whale a Chapter. Before you begin, read Chapter 32 again and note what each sentence in Melville’s account of one whale does. Keep the chapter open while you write if that helps. Here are two of its whales, and its ending.
rules: Write a chapter of this kind about a class of things you know well: dogs, bicycles, the customers of a shop.
Give it a learned title of one word. Begin by saying that nobody has yet put the subject in order.

Divide the subject into three Books and put at least two Chapters in each. You may sort by size, as Melville does, or in some other way. Each Chapter describes one kind of thing and must say how to know that kind when you see it.
End as Melville ends, by leaving the system unfinished and giving a reason why it must be left that way.

Write between 300 and 600 words, which leaves a few sentences for each Chapter. Every fact must be true, and the sentences must sound like Melville’s. The site counts your words, and whether they sound like Melville is for you to judge.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about the Rachel and the end of the book
paras: Auden gives his answer in “The Christian Tragic Hero,” an article he published in *The New York Times Book Review* in 1945. The article sets Greek tragedy against Christian tragedy, the kind to which Ahab belongs. In the first the spectator pities what had to be, and in the second the pity is that it could all have gone otherwise. What was possible for Ahab, Auden says, had limits, because Ahab could not have turned into Ishmael or Starbuck or Pip, or into anyone but Ahab. Auden nevertheless calls Ahab’s possibilities “eternal,” in the sense that the past cannot be altered and yet can always be redeemed in the present. Of the Rachel he says that her captain’s appeal is the last chance offered to Ahab, and that only when Ahab has refused it does his doom become necessary.

In *The Enchafèd Flood*, the book of his 1949 lectures on the sea in Romantic writing, Auden reads the refusal as the last act in a series. All through the voyage, he says, Ahab goes through the acts of a life dedicated to God, but “only for negative reasons.” For example, Ahab gives up his pipe as an ascetic would, but he does it so that nothing will distract him from a task that he and not God has set. Later he puts the boy Pip in the captain’s place in the cabin and goes aloft himself as lookout, a humble post. Auden calls the exchange an inversion of the Gospel saying that whoever would be greatest must be as the least. On the same reading, when Ahab refuses the captain of the Rachel, a neighbor from Nantucket who asks for help in finding his young son, he counterfeits what the Gospel asks of a disciple, who must hate father and mother, wife and children. Auden sums up Ahab’s whole life as one of “taking up defiantly a cross he is not required to take up.” As a result pleasure and pain change places for Ahab, who welcomes the typhoon and treats a calm day as a temptation.

At the end of “The Christian Tragic Hero” Auden writes that Ahab goes to a death he need not have died and drags the crew down with him, and that one man is left, as the chorus is left at the end of a Greek play. But Ishmael, he says, is unlike the Greek chorus, which stands for the average person. Ishmael is not a character at all, because a character is someone who wills and acts, and Ishmael “has no will, only consciousness.” He cannot die, because his life has not started, and Auden pictures him at the end of the book as an infant given back by the sea in Queequeg’s coffin, an orphan “with his first choice still to make.”

Auden puts Ahab’s last chance at the Rachel, in Chapter 128. This site notes that by Auden’s own account the past can always be redeemed, and that in Chapter 132 Starbuck pleads with Ahab to turn the ship for home. In your reply, say whether your paper agrees with Auden about the Rachel. If it does not, say what you would answer him, and if it does, say why Chapter 132 does not change your answer.
sources: “The Christian Tragic Hero,” *The New York Times Book Review*, December 16, 1945, reprinted in *Prose, Volume II*, pp. 258–261.
*The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 138–140.

auden.title: What Auden said in class
paras: Just before playing the record, Auden had assigned *The Castle*, the novel by Franz Kafka that you read next, for the following Tuesday, with questions that you will find in weeks 14 and 15. Donald Pearce, a student in the class who wrote down after lectures what he could remember, reports that Auden talked while he got the record onto the turntable of the portable phonograph he often brought to class. This movement, Auden said, best reflected the relation of an individual to fate, as far as music can express such a relation. He named two cases, the relation “between Ahab and the White Whale” and the relation between K., the main character of Kafka’s novel, and the Castle.

Auden gave no answer to his own question. He started the record, and when it was over he announced a recess of ten minutes. Pearce, who was hearing the recording for the first time, describes what he heard: the piano and the orchestra drawing apart, the piano growing frantic, and at last “the exhausted return, the subdued and poignant close.”

In his account, published in 1985, Pearce says that Auden had made his point very simply, by putting two or three things next to each other in the students’ minds, the books and the music. Pearce adds that he is sure real understanding of anything comes only when things are brought together in that way.
Compare your paper with Pearce’s account of how the movement ends, and say in your reply whether you heard the close as he did.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about the three mates and Pip
paras: In *The Enchafèd Flood*, the book of his 1949 lectures on the sea in Romantic writing, Auden says that the three mates are not evil men. All of them are physically brave and loyal and bear no malice, but all suffer from a sloth of the spirit, which he calls a form of cowardice, and each has refused to grow up. Earlier in the book Auden writes that for Ishmael the voyage of the Pequod means exploring himself and the world. Here he says that each of the mates has set out on that voyage of exploration and then tried to turn back.

Starbuck, Auden says, has gone farthest and suffers most for stopping. He reveres life and death, and takes into his boat only men who are afraid of a whale. Auden adds that Starbuck is the only one of the three who suspects that Ahab’s soul is at risk, and that he is able to tell Ahab the truth to his face. Fear may be the right beginning but will not carry anyone the rest of the way, and mixed with Starbuck’s reverence is a coward’s fear that the whole truth would be more than he could meet. According to Auden, that is why Starbuck believes in omens, and why he does not dare to look closely at the coin.

Stubb has made a religion of being jolly, and anyone who does that, Auden says, cannot face suffering, and must deny it or look the other way. In the coin Stubb reads what suits his view of life and leaves out the rest. He is proud of his kindness, but he is the one who leaves Pip alone in the sea, and the reason Auden gives is that Stubb has never taken a real look at the boy. The best comment on Stubb, he says, is an aphorism of Franz Kafka, the author of *The Castle*, which you read next: everyone is free to keep away from the world’s suffering, but the keeping away may itself be a suffering, and the only one that a person could have avoided.

Auden calls Flask the least likable of the three. Where Stubb looks away from a mystery, Flask denies that there is one. To Flask a whale is a large water-rat, and the coin is a round piece of gold worth sixteen dollars, which will buy nine hundred and sixty cigars. Auden compares what the three mates say as the whale bears down on the ship: Starbuck asks God to stand by him, Stubb wishes for something to eat, and Flask hopes that his mother has drawn his pay.

Auden treats Pip separately from the mates, and pairs him with Ahab. Between them, he says, the two stand for the opposite kinds of despair that Søren Kierkegaard, whose *Fear and Trembling* you read in week 6, defines in another book, *The Sickness unto Death*. Pip’s is the despair of weakness, in which a person does not want to be the self they are, and Ahab’s is the despair of defiance, in which a person insists on being that self. According to Auden, each has met a catastrophe, but Ahab’s madness is turned on the whale and Pip’s on himself. Both would have been saved if Pip had possessed Ahab’s strength and Ahab had possessed Pip’s humility.

If you wrote on one or more of the mates, say in your reply where your account differs from Auden’s and which of the two the book supports. If you wrote on none of them, say whether the fault Auden finds in the mates is in any of your three.
sources: *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 119 and 123–133.

questions.text: This question is for those reading *The Education of Henry Adams*. In Chapter 25, “The Dynamo and the Virgin,” Adams stands before a dynamo at the Paris exposition of 1900 and compares it with the Virgin of Chartres. He calls them both forces. Say what he means by a force, and whether the dynamo and the Virgin are forces in the same sense.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about the Virgin and the Dynamo
paras: Auden took from Chapter 25 of the *Education* the title of “The Virgin & the Dynamo,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). In it he puts Adams’s two figures to his own use. There are two real worlds, he says. The world of the Dynamo is the natural world, which is made of masses and of events that recur, and which can be described only in numbers. The world of the Virgin is the historical world, which is made of faces and of events that happen once, and which can be described only in speech.

Each world, Auden says, has a false copy. The first is made by treating masses as if they were faces, and its religion says prayers to the Dynamo. The second is made by treating faces as if they were masses, and its religion makes a statistic of the Virgin. In both cases, he says, people are trying to avoid being responsible.

Auden then disagrees with Adams, for whom the Virgin of Chartres and Venus were one person. To Auden, Venus is only the Dynamo wearing a disguise, and stands for a natural force that is no person at all. He says that Adams preferred Chartres to Chicago, the city of the 1893 exposition in Chapter 22, only as an aesthete, who liked the disguise better than what it covered, “but it was the Dynamo he worshiped, not the Virgin.”

Auden knew Chapter 25 of the *Education* by 1941, the year of the course. The notes to *New Year Letter*, his long poem published that year, include a sentence copied from that chapter, in which Adams says of Venus and the Virgin that “No American had ever been truly afraid of either.” Auden adds no comment there, but the American edition of the poem lists the *Education* among its modern sources.

Auden quotes the sentence again in “American Poetry,” another essay in *The Dyer’s Hand*, and there he does comment. One reason no American feared either figure, he says, is that the nature Americans had cause to fear could not be imagined as a mother. He offers as a more fitting symbol a white whale that no one can understand, that nobody but a madman such as the Jeroboam’s Gabriel worships, and that can be met only in a fight to the death.

Adams calls both the dynamo and the Virgin forces, but Auden assigns them to two worlds, one described in numbers and the other in speech. In your reply, say whether your paper is closer to Adams or to Auden, and why.

intro: This week you read the one novel of the poet Rainer Maria Rilke, about 190 pages, and the first six chapters of *The Castle*, by the Prague writer Franz Kafka, about 95 more.

Rilke’s novel has no plot. A young Dane, the last of an old family, is alone and poor in Paris. He writes down what he sees in the streets, what he remembers of his childhood, and what he has read. The book was published in German in 1910 and is now known as *The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge*. Auden’s reading list calls it *The Journal of My Other Self*, the title under which W. W. Norton published it in New York in 1930, in the translation by M. D. Herter Norton and John Linton.

In *The Castle* a man called K. arrives in a village as a land surveyor and has to deal with the officials of the Castle. Auden assigned the whole book at one lecture and wanted it read by the following Tuesday. On this site it is spread over two weeks, this one and the next.
The exercise is the last of the three translations, from German.

In the entry that begins “I think I ought to begin to do some work” he lists what a person must have lived through to write a single verse, and then says that even to remember it all is not enough. auden.title: What Auden wrote about this entry and about Rilke’s poetry
paras: Auden put this book on the list, but nothing he said or wrote about it by name has been found. Donald Pearce, a student in the class, believed that the lecture on Shakespeare’s *Henry IV* had gone on to Rilke’s poems the *Duino Elegies*. Pearce kept notes of the lectures, but he was too tired to write that part down at once, and he forgot it before he could.

Auden did praise this entry once, in 1936, in a review of a book in which the English critic Herbert Read defended the Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. Read had quoted the entry in an earlier book. Auden names that book and calls the entry a fine passage on the mass of things seen and heard that ought to go into the making of one poem. He uses the entry against Shelley, who seems to him to have attended in his whole life to nothing but ideas, never to a sight or a sound.

In September 1939 Auden reviewed an English version of the *Duino Elegies* for *The New Republic*. A poet’s standing problem, he says there, is how to put abstract things concretely, and after the seventeenth century hardly anyone found a new way to do it until Rilke. Shakespeare had described what is not human as if it were human, and Rilke does the reverse: he “thinks of the human in terms of the non-human, of what he calls Things (Dinge).” Rilke himself, Auden adds, had pointed out that this is a child’s way of thinking more than an adult’s, since to a child a table, a doll, a tree or a dog is as much alive as the child or the child’s parents.

As this site reads it, Malte’s list is mostly of things seen and heard: cities, animals, birds, roads, rooms, the sea. In your reply, take one item that you said Malte has lived through, and say whether the notebook gives it as something seen and heard or as a feeling. If you go on to this week’s fourth question, on how a poem gets written, keep in mind Malte’s sentence about waiting for memories to come back.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about Rilke
paras: Nothing by Auden about this ending has been found. Auden did review English translations of Rilke twice for *The New Republic* in the two years before the course, and Rilke appears in a long poem that Auden published in 1941.

The first review, of an English translation of Rilke’s poems the *Duino Elegies*, came out in September 1939, in the first week of the war in Europe. Auden says there that it is no accident that writers are more and more drawn, as the crisis between nations worsens, to a poet who “felt that it was pride and presumption to interfere with the lives of others.” Rilke’s reason, as Auden gives it, was that every life is unlike every other, and what looks like its bad luck may be the very road by which it is saved. Auden denies that this turn toward Rilke is defeatism. Writers can do harm to others and to themselves unless they ask, far more humbly than they have been asking, what sort of people they are and what their real work may be. He compares the case to a ship on fire, where running to the pumps may only add to the panic, and sitting still to pray, which looks selfish, may be the most useful thing to do.

The second review, in July 1940, covers two books in English, a selection of fifty of Rilke’s poems and a volume of his letters of 1914 to 1921 called *Wartime Letters of Rainer Maria Rilke*. Rilke, Auden reports, refused to read the newspapers and sat the war out in Munich. By Rilke’s own account, not understanding the war was all that occupied him in those years. “To call this an ivory-tower attitude would be a cheap and wicked lie,” Auden writes. He says that everyone who stays at home in a war feels guilty at being spared, and that the guilt can be paid off in patriotic hatred. To refuse that payment knowingly is itself an act, and it takes great courage. With a second war under way, he recommends Rilke as a writer to go to for strength and not for comfort.

In *New Year Letter*, the long poem Auden published in 1941, the Devil is a tempter who argues with the poet. When the poet starts to protest, the Devil hands him a volume of Rilke and quotes, in German, lines from the *Duino Elegies* on the bliss of the creature that never has to leave the womb. He then points out that in English *womb* rhymes with *tomb*. As this site reads the scene, the Devil is tempting the poet with the wish to be that creature. In a lecture of 1956 Auden said that he still thought Rilke a great poet but could no longer read him.

In your reply, set the son’s plea beside the review of 1939 and the poem of 1941. Say whether the son is asking his family for what Auden admired in Rilke in 1939, a refusal to interfere in another person’s life, or whether his plea is closer to the wish that the Devil holds out to the poet in the poem.

auden.title: What Auden told the class, and wrote elsewhere
paras: Auden did not keep to the order of his reading list in class. The lecture at which he assigned *The Castle* is the earliest that Donald Pearce, a student in the class, recorded in connected notes. Auden had been speaking of Augustine and then of the philosopher Descartes. He questioned Descartes’s “I think, therefore I am” on the ground that modern psychology finds many selves in one person, and no one of them can claim to be the “I” that does the thinking. Of all modern writers, he said, Kafka best expresses that predicament, and in *The Castle* above all.

Auden told the class that “a satire of modern European bureaucracy” was only the book’s disguise. It is in fact, he said, a theological and psychological parable, and it is to the twentieth century what Dante’s poem was to the fourteenth. The class was to read it with the *Divine Comedy* beside it, and to ask where the interests of the two books are alike, where they differ, and why. Then he asked the question about Virgil, and after it he told them to keep Melville in mind as well. He went on to three questions about Ahab and K., and the last of them is the first question of week 15.

He had made the comparison with Dante in *The New Republic* in February 1941: “Had one to name the artist who comes nearest to bearing the same kind of relation to our age that Dante, Shakespeare and Goethe bore to theirs, Kafka is the first one would think of.”

No answer of Auden’s to the question about Virgil has been found, but “The I Without a Self,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), nearly answers it. In the old stories of a quest, the essay says, the hero does not know the way, but others do, and they tell him exactly how to go and what to look out for. In a story by Kafka some of the people the hero meets try to help him, more get in his way, and most do not care, “and none has the faintest notion of the way.” Auden quotes one of Kafka’s aphorisms: “There is a goal but no way; what we call the way is mere wavering.” As this site reads the essay, the answer to Auden’s question would be no. Dante’s Virgil knows the way, and in a story by Kafka, as Auden describes it, nobody does. In your reply, say whether your paper gave the same answer and for the same reason.

auden.title: What Auden said about the telephone
paras: Auden made the remark about the telephone in the spring of 1942, in a second course he taught at Michigan, on the analysis of poetry. Donald Pearce, a student in the fall course, was not enrolled in the second but sat in on a class. The class was discussing “The Solitary Reaper,” William Wordsworth’s poem about a girl who sings as she reaps alone, and Auden asked Pearce what he made of the girl. For the fall course Pearce had written an essay on *The Castle* that found a symbol in nearly everything in the book. He said that the girl was a symbol, and when Auden asked of what, he suggested the peasantry, or rural England.

Auden thought for a moment, walked to the windows, and began: “A poem is a marriage of a poet’s conscious mind and his daemon.” By the daemon he meant the poet’s genius. He spoke of it as something a poet has to get in touch with, and whose existence the poet never doubts, even at the start of a career when there is little to show for it. A poet reaches the daemon neither by will alone nor by chance alone, but by something more like an act of faith. He compared the attempt to telephoning a friend when you cannot for the moment recall the number and will not look it up, so that you try the digits in one order after another until you have them right.

In *The Castle*, he said, the village is the conscious mind and the Castle is the unconscious. Kafka pictures the link between them as a telephone exchange that sometimes works beautifully and often fails, or works without reason, with calls that go astray and messages that can only half be made out. Auden said that he knew no better analogy for the composing of a poem, at the start or while it is going on.

At many points in writing a poem, he said, every poet asks Wordsworth’s question, “Will no one tell me what she sings?” Auden put it as a caller on a bad telephone line would: “Can you speak a little louder?” The girl in the poem, he then told the class, is Wordsworth’s own poetic genius, his daemon.

In the fall course Auden had called *The Castle* a theological and psychological parable, and what he said about the telephone belongs to the psychological reading. The theological reading comes with the second question of week 15.
sources: Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” p. 135 and pp. 154–156.

units.title: *The Castle*. *The Family Reunion*
units.sub: Kafka: *The Castle*, Chapters 7 to 18. Eliot: *The Family Reunion*
intro: In this last week of reading you finish *The Castle*, of which about 180 pages remain. Kafka died in 1924 without finishing the book, and his friend Max Brod, to whom he had left his papers, had the manuscript printed two years later. The translation of 1930, which is the one printed here, follows that first edition and stops at the end of Chapter 18.

T. S. Eliot’s play *The Family Reunion* is still in copyright in the United States, so it is not printed here. If you did not get a copy last week, get one now. The note under the play in the reading list below has a link for borrowing it from the Internet Archive. The play runs to about 75 pages. It was published in 1939, two years before the course, which makes it the newest of the required books.

Wagner’s opera *Götterdämmerung*, which takes about four and a half hours to hear, is also assigned this week. The exercise is a chart that Auden wrote across the blackboard near the end of the term. *Paradiso* XXXIII is due at the end of the week. The examination, five cantos of the *Divine Comedy* written from memory in three hours, falls on the same day, though you may take it earlier or later.

paras: *Götterdämmerung* runs about four and a half hours, in a prelude and three acts. The English translation printed here calls it *The Twilight of the Gods*.

*Götterdämmerung* closes the cycle of four operas called *The Ring of the Nibelung* and is the only part of the cycle on the list. Wagner wrote the words himself, in German. He began in 1848 with a plan for a single opera about the death of the hero Siegfried, which became this one, and then wrote the words of the other three, working backward through the story. All four were first staged together at Bayreuth in August 1876.

You are reading only the end of the story, but in three places the characters tell part of what has gone before: the three Norns, who spin the rope of fate, in the Prelude; Waltraute, one of the Valkyries (the women warriors of the god Wotan), who comes to her sister Brünnhilde, the heroine, in Act 1; and Siegfried himself in Act 3.
While you listen, notice which characters know what is going to happen, and what each of them does about it.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about the opera
paras: In “Mimesis and Allegory,” a lecture given at Columbia University in September 1940 and printed the next year, Auden says that the *Ring* is, in general, about an old order coming to its end. A historian, he says, can read it as Germany in the nineteenth century, with the gods as a reactionary nobility, the dwarfs as a money-grabbing middle class, and the giants as a strong and stupid working class. On that reading a fearless hero and an emancipated woman, Siegfried and Brünnhilde, deliver the country from all three. (In this opera the gods are only talked about until their hall is seen burning at the end, the giants are dead, and the dwarfs are represented by Alberich and by Hagen, his son by a mortal mother.)

That reading runs into trouble in this opera, Auden goes on. “Siegfried and Brünnhilde do not create the new world, they go up in flames with the old.” The ring goes back to the Rhine. The audience is led to expect, he says, that the world will be made new, but nothing definite is said about how or by whom.

Auden also says that the characters behave oddly, and that the oddness does not lie in their making mistakes and paying for those mistakes later. In Sophocles’ tragedy *Oedipus the King*, which is not on the list, Oedipus does not know what he is doing, though the audience does. The characters of the *Ring*, by contrast, are odd because they know in advance that they are making mistakes. They go on predicting the disaster in detail, and “they deny their own knowledge.”

Auden ranks Wagner highest among the Romantic artists in one of the notes he wrote to *New Year Letter*, the long poem he published in the spring of 1941. The reason he gives is that Wagner carries furthest what the note calls the Romantic heresy, “the exaltation of causal necessity over logical necessity.” As this site reads the two terms, causal necessity is the force of what cannot be helped, such as desire or a curse, and logical necessity is the force of a reason that has been thought out. On that reading, characters who know better and go on all the same put the first above the second. Of all the characters in the *Ring*, Auden finds a sign of logic only in Fricka, the goddess of marriage, who does not appear in this opera, and he adds that Wagner makes her unsympathetic.

Another note says that Søren Kierkegaard, whose *Fear and Trembling* you read in week 6, was the first, as far as Auden knew, to mark off tribulations clearly from temptations. A tribulation is a trouble that comes from outside and can only be endured, and a temptation is a conflict within a person that the will has to settle by acting. The note on Wagner calls the operas masterpieces when they are taken as studies in tribulation. Taken as dramatic plots, it says, they are absurd, because the characters know in advance that they are making mistakes, which is the point the lecture had made. The poem describes the Wagnerian hero in a couplet: “His intellectual life fulfilled / In knowing that his doom is willed.”

In a review of 1969 Auden summarizes the theory of opera that Wagner set out in 1851. It allowed no duets or ensembles, gave the work of the chorus to the orchestra, and replaced the set aria with continuous melody. From *Die Meistersinger* (1868) on, Auden says, Wagner dropped the theory altogether and wrote grand opera of the kind the nineteenth century already knew. Auden agrees with Bernard Shaw, the playwright and former music critic, that *Götterdämmerung*, with its poisoned drinks and its ensemble of conspirators, is close kin to Verdi’s opera *Un Ballo in Maschera* (1859).

Before you listened you were asked to notice which characters know what is going to happen, and what each of them does about it. Compare what you noticed with what Auden says the characters know (the third paragraph under this heading), and ask whether what they suffer is a tribulation or a temptation as the note defines the two (the fifth). You do not need to write anything down.

paras: Pearce’s notes give no answer of Auden’s to this question. In assigning the book, Auden had told the class that it was to the twentieth century what Dante’s poem was to the fourteenth, and that they were to read it with the *Divine Comedy* beside it (see the third question of week 14). As soon as he had asked the question at the top of this page, he went to the phonograph, and while he put a record on he named Ahab and the White Whale, and K. and the Castle, as two cases of the relation of an individual to fate. He then played the class the second movement of Beethoven’s Fourth Piano Concerto (see week 13).

In February 1941 Auden reviewed three books by Kafka, *The Castle* among them, in *The New Republic*, under the title “The Wandering Jew.” Kafka’s novels, he says, use the oldest device in literature, the quest, and should be read beside the older quests. The hero of a fairy tale is the lucky third son, and his success is foretold. Later heroes are marked out by being morally better than most people or, like Goethe’s Faust and Ibsen’s Peer Gynt, morally worse. Faust and Peer Gynt have an easy time of it, Auden says, because they take what is arbitrary in themselves for necessary. As this site reads the phrase, they follow their own wishes as though those wishes were laws.

Auden calls K. “the mirror-image of Faust.” The goal of a Kafka hero, he says, is as clear as the goal of the old quests, and everyone recognizes it: in *The Castle*, everyone wants to live near the Castle. For the heroes before K., being exceptional in some way was the one hope of success. K. is exceptional without being able to tell in what way, and for him that is the source of his troubles. Auden then gives what he takes Kafka to be saying: to have faith is to accept something as necessary, to become exceptional is to become reflective, and to a reflective person what is necessary looks arbitrary. On this account Faust has an easy time because he never notices that the thing he obeys is arbitrary, while K. can no longer hide from himself how arbitrary everything looks, and so is always in danger of losing his faith. By that measure, the same passage says, Faust and Peer Gynt were never exceptions. They stand for the ordinary person who does not reflect, if there still is such a person.

Near its end the review says: “Kafka is important to us because the predicament of his hero is the predicament of the contemporary man.” Life in an industrial civilization, Auden adds, turns every person into a K., exceptional and reflective.
In an essay of 1946, “K’s Quest,” Auden says that K. fails because he is an individual, and that “he cannot become what he wishes, the Land Surveyor, because he cannot cease to be K.”

“The I Without a Self,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), says that in a typical story by Kafka the goal is the hero’s alone and that he has no rivals for it, where the review of 1941 had said that everyone recognizes the goal. The essay puts the difference between K. and the heroes before him as two questions. The hero of every earlier quest, Auden says, knows what ought to be done and asks only “Can I do it?” Homer’s Odysseus, for one, knows that he must not heed the Sirens’ song. K.’s question is “What ought I to do?” He is not tempted, Auden says, since to be tempted is to have to choose between good and evil. K. is sure that what he does next matters a great deal, but he has no idea what it should be and can only guess. When his guess is wrong, he suffers what a wrong choice would have brought on him, and he has to feel just as responsible.

The hero of the older quests, Auden goes on, earned by gifts and deeds the right to say “I.” K. starts as an “I,” with no gifts or deeds to show for it, and that alone is his guilt. In *The Castle*, Auden writes, “K, the letter, wants to become a word, land-surveyor.” K. wants a self such as other people have, he explains, and that is what K. is refused.

“The I Without a Self” also warns against interpreting Kafka. He wrote parables, and the essay holds that a parable means something different to each reader. A critic can help other people see what a novel or a play contains, but a critic who sets about interpreting a parable, Auden says, “will only reveal himself.”

Take the paragraphs above as Auden’s own response to the book. This site chose them for what they say about K. On Ahab and on Dante they give only what Auden said to the class when he assigned the book. In your reply, compare what Auden says K. wants with what you wrote, without trying to settle which of you is right.

“K’s Quest,” in *The Kafka Problem*, edited by Angel Flores (New Directions, 1946), reprinted in *Prose, Volume II*, pp. 282–286.
“The I Without a Self,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 159–160 and 162–163.

questions.text: Amalia tore up Sortini’s letter. The Castle did nothing to her family, and the village ruined it. Max Brod, who edited the book, compared her case with Abraham’s in *Fear and Trembling*. Does the comparison hold?
gloss: Read Chapter 15, all five parts. Brod’s note, which stands at the end of the first American edition of 1930, is not printed here. In it he says that the Castle is nearly what theologians mean by grace. Grace, as he explains it, is God’s guidance of human destiny, which sends favors and punishments alike and can be neither earned nor reached. He compares Sortini’s letter with the command to Abraham: God asked of Abraham what was a crime, and the official asks of the girl what is plainly immoral. You read Kierkegaard on Abraham in week 6.

auden.title: What Auden said and wrote about the Castle and its officials
paras: The first American edition of 1930 has two notes that are left out here. Edwin Muir, one of the translators, says at the front that the subject of the novel is human life as it is acted on by “divine law and divine grace,” and he proposes reading it as a modern version of *Pilgrim’s Progress*, John Bunyan’s allegory of 1678. At the back is the note by Brod described under the question, which takes the Castle for grace and compares Sortini’s letter with the command to Abraham.

In 1941, at the lecture where Auden assigned the book, he told the class that it was a theological and psychological parable, and that it was to the twentieth century what Dante’s poem was to the fourteenth. In the notes of Donald Pearce, a student in the class who wrote down after lectures what he could remember, Auden does not say what the Castle stands for in theology. Later in the same lecture he named Ahab and the White Whale, and K. and the Castle, as two cases of the relation of an individual to fate (see the second question of week 13). The next spring Pearce heard him say that the Castle is the unconscious and the village the conscious mind (see the fourth question of week 14).

Auden argues against the reading of the Castle as grace in “The I Without a Self,” an essay in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962). With a writer of parables such as Kafka, he says, facts about the author’s life are a great help, if only by ruling out false readings. He then describes a Czech novel, Božena Němcová’s *The Grandmother*, of which Brod gives an account in a new edition of his life of Kafka. In Němcová’s novel the village lies under a castle whose owner, a duchess, is kind, while the officials and servants who stand between her and the villagers are shown as plainly bad. Auden takes this to suggest that the critics who saw servants of God’s grace in the people of Kafka’s Castle had read the book wrongly, and that the reading of the critic Erich Heller is right in the main. He quotes Heller, who calls the Castle the garrison “of a company of Gnostic demons,” holding its ground against an impatient soul. (The Gnostics were sects of the first Christian centuries who taught that hostile powers stand between the soul and the true God.) The Castle’s officers, Heller says, “are totally indifferent to good if they are not positively wicked,” and they arouse dread and disgust but no reverence.

“The I Without a Self” does not mention Amalia or Sortini. The link between Amalia’s case and what the essay says about the officials is this site’s. In your reply, say what becomes of Brod’s comparison if the officials are what Heller and Auden take them to be, and whether Amalia’s refusal then looks different from Abraham’s obedience.
sources: Edwin Muir’s Introductory Note and Max Brod’s Additional Note, in Kafka, *The Castle* (Knopf, 1930).
Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” pp. 135–136 and 155.
“The I Without a Self,” in *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 160–161.

questions.text: At the end of the play Harry leaves Wishwood to follow the Eumenides, and the house goes to his brother John. Why is Harry called, and not John?
gloss: The word “called” is Auden’s. He uses it in the religious sense, of a person chosen for a way of life and summoned to it. The Eumenides come from the *Oresteia* of Aeschylus, a set of three plays of which *Agamemnon*, one of the two tragedies offered in week 2, is the first. At the end of the third, the Furies, who have hunted Agamemnon’s son Orestes for killing his mother, are turned into the Kindly Ones, which is what the name Eumenides means. Decide whether Eliot’s Eumenides change in the course of the play, or whether Harry does.

auden.title: What Auden wrote about the play
paras: No writing of Auden’s about the play from the years of the course has been found.

The nearest thing is a note to *New Year Letter*, Auden’s long poem of 1941. The note is about American literature as a whole and does not mention the play. It places Eliot in an American line with Poe, Emerson, Hawthorne, Melville and Henry James, says that this tradition stands much closer to Dostoevsky than to Tolstoy, and calls it “a literature of lonely people.” Ask yourself whether Harry, who leaves his family at the end of the play, is one of the lonely people the note speaks of.

Reviewing Eliot’s collected poems and plays in 1953, Auden hears a snobbish note now and then in this play and in another of Eliot’s plays, *The Cocktail Party* (1949), and he puts it down to technique. Eliot, Auden says, wanted a verse for the stage that would not be arty, and had put off the problem of a dramatic convention. He did so by keeping, just as he found them, the long-standing conventions of English high comedy, in which the scene and the leading characters belong to the aristocracy. So long as the subject is a worldly one, such as love between a man and a woman, and the values are social, those conventions work perfectly well, Auden says, because riches and good breeding can stand for gifts and virtues. They fail once the theme is spiritual election (the calling of one person and not another) and the gulf that separates Christian faith from every worldly value. He is “absolutely certain” that Eliot did not mean the audience to think “that Harry is called and not John because John is stupid.” But the convention of comedy that Eliot works in, he says, cannot help giving the audience that idea.

Auden wrote about Harry again in the foreword to *Secondary Worlds* (1968), the book of the lectures he gave in Eliot’s memory in 1967. He notes that the hero of Eliot’s first full-length play, *Murder in the Cathedral* (1935), was a martyr known to history, Thomas Becket, the archbishop of Canterbury who was killed in his cathedral in 1170. The audience is not told what happens to Harry, Auden says, but Harry “decides to take up a way of life which may well lead” to martyrdom.

In your reply, say whether the reason you gave in your paper is the one that Auden rules out in the review of 1953. If it is, say whether the play suggested it to you in the way he describes, and if it is not, say whether anything in the play could lead an audience to the reason he rules out.
sources: *New Year Letter* (Faber and Faber, 1941), the note to line 1566.

“T. S. Eliot So Far,” *The Griffin*, March 1953, reprinted in *A Company of Readers*, edited by Arthur Krystal (Free Press, 2001), pp. 225–228. The two phrases quoted are also in a note on p. 473 of Edward Mendelson’s *Early Auden, Later Auden* (Princeton University Press, 2017).

questions.text: The course is called “Fate and the Individual in European Literature.” Take three of its books, from three different centuries. In each, say what the individual is up against, and whether that individual could have done otherwise.
gloss: One way to choose is to take one book from before 1700, one from the nineteenth century and one from the twentieth.

auden.title: What Auden said and wrote that bears on the title
paras: No statement by Auden of what the title meant, or of why he chose these books, has been found. Charles Miller, who was in the class, remembered forty years later that on the first day Auden spoke of “our theme of fate and the individual in European literature.”

In an article of March 1941, “James Joyce and Richard Wagner,” Auden says that the art of every age down to about 1850 was built on two contrasts. The first sets order and free will against chaos and fate, and the second sets the hero against the churl. The churl is “the passive slave of circumstance.” Heroes pit their will against accident and make order for themselves and for others, but heroism has a price: “to choose to do or think something means to choose not to do or think anything else.” As an example he gives Antigone, the heroine of the tragedy by Sophocles that was one of the two offered in week 2. She cannot both keep the law and do what she owes her brother, and knowing this she makes her choice and wills her death. The disorder is in her situation, he says, and not in her.

A month earlier, in a review of Kafka called “The Wandering Jew,” Auden had told the history of one kind of hero, the one who goes on a quest. In the fairy tale he is the third son, and his success is foretold. Galahad, the knight who attains the Holy Grail in the medieval legend, and Christian, the pilgrim of John Bunyan’s *Pilgrim’s Progress* (1678), are marked out, Auden says, by being morally better than most people. Goethe’s Faust and Ibsen’s Peer Gynt are marked out by being morally worse: “The Hero has become a Bohemian.” The last is K., who is marked out but cannot tell in what way. Faust, Peer Gynt and K. are heroes of books on the list, where they come in the same order (weeks 6, 7 and 14 on this site). On the published copy of the list, though, *Faust* is marked “Omit.” Nothing has been found in which Auden says that he built the course from the review.

In class Auden played the second movement of Beethoven’s Fourth Piano Concerto. The piano, he said, defies the orchestra as a person defies fate, and he asked whether the piano found its way back too late (see week 13). In 1945 he called Greek tragedy the tragedy of necessity, in which what happens had to happen, and Christian tragedy the tragedy of possibility, in which it could have been otherwise (see the third question of week 11). What he wrote in 1948 on Greek and modern tragedy is reported under the first question of week 2 and the second and third questions of week 4. In your reply, apply the contrast between necessity and possibility to the last clause of the question. Say for each of your three books whether what happened had to happen.

making.title: The chart of the course
making.short: Nine pairs of terms from Auden’s blackboard: find a book, an author or a character for each term
brief: Auden did not keep to the order of the reading list in class, and he lectured on *The Tempest* near the end of the term. At the close of that lecture, before he told the class about the examination, he went to the blackboard and copied out a chart he had made for them. It was in two lines, one above the other, and when he had finished it ran the whole width of the room. Donald Pearce, a student in the class who wrote down after lectures what he could remember, reports him saying that it was “a summary of certain themes and relationships we had been concerned with during the semester.”

Pearce did not have to remember the chart, because he copied it down as Auden wrote it. It has nine pairs of terms, with one term of each pair in the upper line and the other below it. Pearce gives the terms without explaining them and without naming any books, so there is no key.
rules: For each pair, name a book, an author or a character from the reading of all fifteen weeks for the upper term and another for the lower, counting an opera as a book.
Give your reason in a sentence. If a term is not plain to you, add a few words on what you take it to mean.
Use at least ten different books in all. Characters count as the books they are in. An author counts as one book, in addition to any book by that author that you name elsewhere.
Fill at least fourteen of the eighteen boxes. The other four may stay empty if you cannot place a term.

A larger chart of the same kind survives. Auden wrote it out for a seminar on Romanticism at Swarthmore College in 1943, and [the college has published it](https://archive.swarthmore.edu/auden/romanticism.html).

pieces.title: The words over the gate of Hell
pieces.cite: Dante, Inferno III, lines 1 to 9, in Longfellow’s translation
why: The gate speaks for itself, in the first person. Its first three lines open with the same four words, the next three say who made it, and the ninth is the best-known line in the poem. They are also the opening of one of the cantos Auden set.

syllabus.title: The reading list
intro: A mimeographed reading list survives from the course. The standard bibliography of Auden, by Bloomfield and Mendelson, describes it as two sheets. Alan Jacobs, a scholar of Auden, published a picture of the first sheet in 2012 with the permission of Auden’s estate, and [it can be seen on his site](https://blog.ayjay.org/audensyllabus/).

The list is headed English 135, Fate and the Individual in European Literature. Under the title it gives the particulars: first semester, two hours of credit, Thursdays from four to six in 2215 Angell Hall, open to juniors, seniors and graduate students who have the written permission of Professor Arno Bader. The instructor’s name is typed as “W. Auden.” The list carries no year, and the standard bibliography puts it in the fall semester of 1941.
The three tables below keep the order of the list. For every required book and opera they give the edition (where the list names one), the text this site prints, and the week you read it in.

required.title: Required reading
intro: The list has twenty-three entries of required reading. One entry offers a choice between *Agamemnon* and *Antigone*, and you pick one when you reach week 2. On the published sheet someone has written “Omit” by hand beside two others, *Faust* and *The Education of Henry Adams*. Who wrote it is not recorded. This site prints both books but does not require them. It leaves them out of the weekly page count and the tests, and you never have to write a paper on either.

opera.title: Opera libretti
intro: The list assigns nine opera libretti as reading. Donald Pearce, who took the course, remembers that Auden brought a phonograph and records to class. On this site you read each libretto and then listen to the whole opera with the libretto open. The site has no recordings, so you will need to find a complete recording of each opera, and a public library or a streaming service is the likely place to look. The shortest of the nine runs about an hour and a half and the longest about four and a half hours.

The list names no editions of the libretti. Most of the texts printed here are the English versions from the bilingual libretti that Fred Rullman of New York published. Where the table names no translator, the libretto names none. The operas themselves are in Italian, German or French. Unless your recording is sung in English, you will hear one of those languages and follow the sense in the text printed here.

critical.title: Recommended critical reading
intro: The list recommends eighteen books of criticism. Nothing assigned on this site depends on them, and none of them is printed here. Where one is out of copyright in the United States and this site found a free copy online, the table links to it.

The first sheet ends after the eighth of them, so the published picture shows only those eight. The other ten are known from Charles Miller, who took the course and prints the list in his memoir. The list gets three of the authors’ names wrong, and Miller’s copy has slips of its own. This site corrects both kinds of error.

about.title: What is on record and what this site supplied
about.lede: What is known of English 135 comes from the reading list, from notes that two students, Donald Pearce and Kenneth Millar, made in 1941, and from accounts that students wrote many years later. Whatever on this site does not come from them is reconstruction. The site was made by Claude, an AI system, and no Auden scholar has checked it.

paras: Three students who took the course wrote about it later: Donald Pearce, Charles Miller and Robert Chapman. A fourth, Kenneth Millar, went on to write detective novels as Ross Macdonald. Tom Nolan’s biography of Millar and Michael Kreyling’s study of the novels describe his part in the course. Dorothy Farnan was a graduate student at Michigan who knew people in the class. Humphrey Carpenter wrote a biography of Auden, and B. C. Bloomfield and Edward Mendelson compiled the standard bibliography of his writings. Mendelson also edited Auden’s collected prose, the second volume of which is cited here as *Prose, Volume II*. The accounts are cited below by the author’s surname and the page, and Works cited, near the bottom of this page, gives each reference in full.

In the spring of 1942 Auden gave a second course at Michigan, English 136, on the analysis of poetry. The last two rows of the table below report work that the sources do not assign to one course or the other.

paras: Donald Pearce wrote the fullest account of the course more than forty years later, with his notes from 1941 in front of him. He says that in December, four or five weeks before the examination, Auden told the class what it would be. The examination would last three hours and would come after the Christmas vacation. The class would write out, from memory, seven cantos in the prose version that Pearce calls Carlyle and Wicksteed’s. That is the translation by Carlyle, Okey and Wicksteed in the Modern Library volume named on the list. The cantos began with *Inferno* III and V, continued with some from the *Purgatorio* (Pearce names only XXVIII) and ended with *Paradiso* XXXIII. A committee of students called the task impossible. Auden cut the seven cantos to five, and said that if he could not learn the five himself on his drive to California he would telephone and cancel the examination. He did not telephone, and Pearce wrote for three hours and filled five blue books.

Charles Miller, also in the class, remembers the cantos being assigned at the first meeting as an exercise: six, or four for those who could not manage six. Dorothy Farnan, who had the story from friends in the class, says six, assigned on the first day for the final examination and to be learned letter perfect. Tom Nolan, in his biography of Kenneth Millar, says that in place of a final Auden had the students memorize “any six Dante cantos.”

Robert Chapman took both of Auden’s Michigan courses, and in 1978 he printed what his classmates remembered. Some of them claimed that they still had eight cantos by heart. One ran out of time at the final examination for the fall course before she had written out all her Dante, and left the note “Time.” Auden telephoned to ask whether that was the truth, accepted that it was, and did not penalize her.

So two people who were in the class, Pearce and Chapman, say that the cantos were written out at a timed examination. The number of cantos is given as five by Pearce, six by Farnan and Nolan, six or four by Miller, and eight by some of Chapman’s classmates. This site follows Pearce, the only one to name the translation, the length of the examination and any of the cantos. He names four of the seven that Auden first asked for but does not say which two were dropped, so the site keeps those four and you choose the fifth yourself on the [By heart](#/heart) page.

The list gives no dates. This site takes the books in the order of the list and divides them among fifteen weeks. Counting one Greek play and the nine libretti, and leaving out the two books marked “Omit,” the reading comes to about 280 pages a week.

Auden did not keep to the order of the list, but the order he followed is known only in part, so this site could not follow it. Pearce’s notes, as far as they go, give this sequence of lectures: Augustine and Kafka; romantic love, with *Tristan und Isolde* and *Carmen*; *Othello*; *Henry IV*; and in December *The Tempest*. In the first of those lectures Auden introduced Kafka and assigned *The Castle* for the following Tuesday, telling the class to read it with Dante and Melville in mind. The class had a week at most to read it; this site allows two weeks.

No week-by-week record of the course has been published. Auden is known to have given a class most of the kinds of work on this site, at Michigan or elsewhere, and the table below says where. The two exceptions are the charts and the parody, and the table explains each. The particular passages and exercises, and all but six of the questions, were chosen by this site.

Auden taught for four weeks in 1939 at St. Mark’s School in Massachusetts. After Michigan he taught at Swarthmore College from 1942 to 1945, and in 1946 and 1947 he lectured on Shakespeare at the New School in New York.
